editorials.title: More heft: On India and the 18th BRICS Summit
editorials.passage:
Forging a joint statement at a major multilateral conference, in the midst of global conflicts where members are involved is never easy — for India, hosting the BRICS Summit in Delhi is the second time in recent years, since the G-20 Summit in 2023, that it has had to shoulder such a responsibility. That, however, is not the only reason India’s BRICS presidency comes at a difficult time. The past few occasions India has hosted the coalition of emerging economies — in 2012, 2016 and virtually in 2021 — it was a smaller grouping of just five major powers, where managing consensus was easier. Since the expansion in 2024 — adding Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE — and Indonesia’s induction in 2025, BRICS’ identity has evolved, but a common focus remains elusive. In addition, global conflicts involving BRICS members have grown. The war involving Iran has heightened this impact, as Iran, a victim of the U.S.-Israel strikes, as well as the UAE that was attacked by Iran in retaliation, are members that have been unwilling to agree to a common narrative on the problem. India’s position on Israel also came into conflict with other members earlier this year, as the grouping has traditionally taken a much more critical line on Israel’s actions. The largest share of New Delhi’s problems as host comes however from the United States, where President Donald Trump has accused it of plotting to overthrow the U.S. dollar’s domination of the global economy, and has been threatening tariffs on all members for planning to increase intra-BRICS payments and trade. As the Modi government seeks to restore ties with the Trump administration, on trade and its Indo-Pacific strategy, hosting BRICS also risks invoking America’s ire, however irrational.

As a result, a success in reconciling all these different strands at this time would indeed be a shot across the bow for the grouping and a big win for Indian diplomacy. Since it was first conceptualised 25 years ago, and a summit convened in 2009, the BRICS countries have risen in global stature and economic heft, benefitting intra-BRICS trade. Today, BRICS accounts for half the world’s population, two fifths of the global economy and a fourth of global trade; it also includes many of the world’s top energy producers and biggest consumers. While the grouping prefers not to be called anti-western it is certainly a powerful counter to the G-7, and western-led thinking. Being part of BRICS gives India more heft in advancing its ambitions on the global high table, and its presidency has ensured it prominence on the world stage, as leaders and representatives of 11 BRICS countries including Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Masoud Pezeshkian begin deliberations on Saturday at the Bharat Mandapam to discuss the future of global governance.

editorials.title: Eyes on the road: On India and road traffic fatalities
editorials.passage:
Despite hosting only 1% of the world’s vehicular fleet, India accounts for around 11% of road traffic fatalities , due in some part to widespread non-compliance with wearing seat belts and helmets while driving. Post-crash investigations have often revealed victims being ejected from vehicles or suffering lethal secondary collisions against vehicles’ interiors; children are also vulnerable due to the patchy use of child restraint systems and rear-seat belts. Recently, a Supreme Court Bench asked the Road Transport Ministry to consider a petition to reduce road traffic deaths by habituating the use of these measures . Actual policing is certainly wanting, including due to chronic shortages of traffic police cadres; there is also room to constrain manufacturers to install tamper-proof seat belt reminders and thwart modifications after purchase. The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019 instituted or scaffolded various mechanisms to prevent road traffic deaths whereas the national data so far have not presented evidence of improvement at the scale India needs.

However, in 2024, Road Transport Ministry data said that two-wheeler riders constituted 46.2% and pedestrians 20.6% of road deaths . Seat belts and child restraints only protect occupants of enclosed vehicles, so better enforcing their adoption will address the reasons underlying only one-third of the total mortality. In fact, speeding has been found to be the dominant recorded violation associated with fatalities, and a national strategy focused on mitigating opportunities for vehicles to accelerate to high speeds may yield greater gains. Second, neither the Union government nor State governments have systematically employed the ‘Safe System’ approach. While individual responsibility and the duty of care accruing to schools and similar institutions matter, governments are still expected to design roads assuming that not everyone will behave perfectly. Put differently, they need to reduce the probability as well as the severity of crashes, including by identifying and fixing accident-prone locations, setting up physical environments that compensate for human error, reducing children’s exposure to two-wheeler traffic, and improving timely access to trauma care. Finally, India lacks a public culture that reinforces safe behaviour and deters unsafe behaviour. For India to reduce road mortality in a sustained manner, governments must treat safety through a combination of approaches that does not overstate the role of individual decisions. It is also commendable that the Court has referred the petition to the Centre, rather than assume an interventionist posture as it did in 2019, in a tacit acknowledgment that road safety has outgrown judicial fiat.

editorials.title: Following robust tax growth, GST Council needs to plug leakages
editorials.passage: Even as the controversy surrounding India’s GDP data remains unsettled, accusations are being raised against the authenticity of GST collections. The monthly indirect tax haul is growing in healthy double-digits, outpacing nominal GDP growth. However, former Finance Secretary Subash Chandra Garg has levelled fresh allegation that the net GST collection—stripping out tax credits and refunds—was registering lower growth than the nominal GDP. Moreover, by his calculations, if we exclude GST compensation cess, which was discontinued in September 2025, the overall growth in tax collection would remain sub-par.The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs was quick to dismiss Garg’s allegations as misleading and mischievous for cherry-picking figures from two different tax bases and raising suspicion when there’s none. Further, it argued that it has been transparently publishing data pertaining to compensation cess in separate tables, with detailed disclosures. Garg countered that the increasing tendency to manage data to suit narratives is unfortunate..Comparing current revenue against past data with discontinued levies and calling the difference a statistical trickery is a classic accounting mistake. Even if Garg rejects the government’s claim about double-digit expansion in monthly GST revenue as a sign of robust economic activity, it’s undeniable that the money is flowing to the exchequer. There is simply no merit for the government to inflate tax revenue data and complicate its income and expenditure budget. Moreover, the annual growth in both gross and net GST collections is below nominal GDP growth. For instance, in 2025-26, gross collections at ₹22.27 lakh crore saw 8.3 percent growth, while net proceeds at ₹19.34 lakh crore registered a 7.1 percent increase. These are actual monies collected and refunded, and tax officials have no benefit in reporting otherwise.The allegations have come close to next month’s GST Council meeting. At this, the council’s first huddle since the major rate rationalisation exercise last year, it must speed up work on simplifying refunds and speeding up registrations. One focus should be preventing fake input tax credit claims, which are alarmingly rising. In 2025-26 alone, authorities detected 30,000-odd such cases worth ₹74,782 crore. Fake invoicing and fraudulent claims lead to significant revenue leakage. editorials.title: Make space for film lovers of all means
editorials.passage: The Thiruvananthapuram mayor’s recent exclamation—“A movie ticket for ₹200 and popcorn for ₹500!”—has reignited a much-needed discussion about the exorbitant cost a family incurs when it decides to watch a movie at a theatre. While questioning the hefty prices of what’s sold inside, Mayor V V Rajesh also called out the restrictions on carrying in food and drinking water from outside. Thankfully, he did not stop at that and directed all theatres in the city to ensure clean drinking water dispensers near entrances and exits. Cinema halls have also been warned against stopping parents from bringing essential food items for young children. The mayor has given theatre owners 15 days to act on these fronts.It’s true that multiplexes have changed the movie-going experience. The transition from single-screen halls to multiplex screening has also raised operational costs, which theatre owners try to recoup with overpriced food and beverages. But none of these should cost so high that they would burn holes in the pockets of film lovers..Theatre owners peg their argument to a recent Supreme Court verdict striking down a Jammu and Kashmir High Court order removing restrictions on movie-goers bringing in food. The SC had also allowed theatre owners to fix the price of refreshments. But it had also mandated that free water should be provided and food for infants be allowed in halls. The theatre owners seem to have conveniently forgotten that part of the order serving their patrons’ basic needs.Whatever be the legal reading, it should not stop anyone—especially elected representatives—from calling out a level of pricing that affects the public. Big-screen viewing should not be the sole preserve of well-to-do households. Such exclusionary practice has larger implications, too. The affordability crisis is deterring most Indian families from flocking to big screens, which in turn directly dampens the prospects of the film exhibition and distribution segments, on which a large number of livelihoods depend. Things have come to such a pass that a wider consensus on pricing food and beverages is called for—keeping in mind the interests of both audiences and entrepreneurs. editorials.title: Quick Take | Shaming into action
editorials.passage: The residents of Anuppur—a district in eastern Madhya Pradesh known for being home to Amarkantak, where the Narmada and Son rivers originate—have staged a unique protest. In a video that has elicited a splash of comments, dozen-odd men are seen lounging about in ankle-deep water amid a massive pothole. A few months ago, youngsters in Assam’s Cachar district recorded several videos of dancing in muddy puddles along National Highway 6, a lifeline for the Northeast. Potholes claim thousands of Indian lives every year. Perhaps the well-minded techies who built the Pothole Fix and Pothole Reporter apps can expand their scope to allow pinning such crowd-sourced shaming videos with geolocation data from across the country. editorials.title: Together let’s rejuvenate ‘untidy’ ocean tides
Reason for optimism
editorials.passage:
India and China may finally be trying to turn the page on years of border confrontation. After the 2020 military crisis, prolonged deployment along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and a deep deterioration in political trust, the two countries are cautiously rebuilding their relationship. The latest Special Representatives’ talks between National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi are particularly significant because the focus appears to be shifting from simply managing the disputed border to discussing boundary delimitation. 

The reference to an “early and substantial harvest” is encouraging. But India should judge the process by concrete outcomes, not diplomatic formulations. For years, New Delhi and Beijing tried to separate the boundary dispute from the broader relationship. Trade expanded, economic engagement deepened and both countries worked together in forums such as BRICS and other multilateral institutions. The assumption was that growing economic interdependence could help insulate bilateral ties from the unresolved border question. The 2020 Ladakh crisis demonstrated the weakness of that assumption. 

The violent confrontation and subsequent military mobilisation transformed the relationship. Mutual trust declined sharply, and the border became the central determinant of bilateral ties. The disengagement process that followed has reduced immediate risks, but it has not removed the underlying dispute. This is why the renewed Special Representatives’ dialogue is important. Existing mechanisms - including military commander-level meetings, diplomatic consultations and the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination ~ have helped prevent incidents from escalating. 

Additional communication mechanisms, including proposed meeting points for senior commanders and hotlines in the Eastern and Middle Sectors, can further reduce the possibility of accidental conflict. But there is a fundamental limit to such arrangements: a disputed boundary cannot be managed indefinitely. Crisis-management mechanisms can prevent clashes, but they cannot resolve the territorial dispute that produces them. The proposed “early harvest” therefore deserves serious attention. The Expert Group on Boundary Delimitation and the Working Group on Border Management are expected to take the process forward. The immediate task will be to establish their terms of reference. Yet the crucial questions are political rather than procedural. 

Which areas will be included in the early harvest? On what principles will they be selected? Will limited agreements represent genuine progress towards a final settlement, or merely create another layer of border management? India must ensure that the latter does not happen. The reaffirmation of the 2005 Agreement on Political Parameters and Guiding Principles provides an important foundation. That agreement envisaged a framework for resolving the boundary dispute, followed by delineation and demarcation. Rather than creating an entirely new diplomatic architecture, the two sides can build upon this existing framework. 

What is required now is political will to move from general principles to substantive negotiations. There are reasons for cautious optimism. China has an interest in a stable external environment as it deals with wider economic and strategic challenges. India, too, does not want a permanently confrontational relationship with its largest neighbour to consume diplomatic and military resources. Both countries also have incentives to maintain communication through BRICS and other Global South institutions. However, normalisation should not be confused with reconciliation. 

The emerging relationship is more accurately described as competitive coexistence. India and China will continue to compete over influence in South Asia and the Indian Ocean. China’s close relationship with Pakistan, its connectivity initiatives and India’s growing strategic partnerships with the United States and other Indo-Pacific countries will remain sources of friction. A reduction in border tensions will not eliminate these structural differences. The incremental approach advocated by Chinese scholar Hu Shisheng is therefore revealing. 

Institutionalising stability along the LAC and operationalising an “early harvest” may be more acceptable to Beijing than attempting an immediate comprehensive settlement. India should be open to incremental progress, but it must guard against incrementalism becoming an excuse for indefinite delay. Other recent developments can contribute to confidencebuilding. Dialogue on trans-border rivers could address India’s concerns about hydrological data and developments in Tibet. The reopening of border trading points and expansion of the Kailash Manasarovar pilgrimage can also restore some of the practical links disrupted by the deterioration in relations. 

Yet the fragility of the process remains evident. Arunachal Pradesh continues to be a major point of contention, and China’s objections to India’s naming of places in the state demonstrate how quickly territorial sensitivities can revive tensions. Normalisation cannot mean accepting the other side’s territorial claims. Nor should practical cooperation obscure unresolved sovereignty issues. For this reason, transparency in the negotiating process will matter. The details of territorial negotiations will necessarily remain confidential, but governments should communicate the broad principles and objectives of the process. In India especially, any perception of secret territorial concessions could generate political opposition and undermine public support for an eventual agreement. 

The timing of the present diplomatic initiative is also noteworthy. Ajit Doval’s visit to Beijing comes ahead of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi and could create space for political direction at the highest level, including a possible meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping. Such a meeting need not produce a spectacular breakthrough. Its greater value could lie in consolidating the momentum already generated by diplomatic and military contacts. The sequence matters: disengagement, restoration of diplomatic communication, renewed Special Representatives’ talks, discussions on boundary delimitation and possible leader-level engagement. 

Together, these steps suggest an attempt to move from crisis management towards managed competition. But India should remain clear about the destination. Peace on the border and progress on the boundary question must move together. Border stability without substantive negotiations could simply reproduce the pre-2020 model - periodic calm punctuated by renewed confrontation. The road from border management to boundary settlement will undoubtedly be long and difficult. Territorial disputes between major powers are rarely resolved quickly. 

But the present moment offers an opportunity that should not be wasted. If the “early harvest” is given a clear mandate, defined areas, a realistic timetable and a direct link to the larger boundary settlement, it could become more than another confidence-building exercise. The real test of India-China normalisation is therefore not whether the border becomes quiet, but whether the two countries can use that quiet to address the dispute itself. A stable LAC should be the beginning of boundary negotiations, not their substitute. 

(The writer is Associate Fellow, Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defense Studies and Analyses)

editorials.title: When celebration pollutes the night
editorials.passage:
Environmental protection has traditionally focused on measurable pollutants such as contaminated air, polluted rivers, toxic soil, excessive noise, and hazardous chemicals. While these remain critical concerns, an equally important but largely ignored form of environmental degradation is silently spreading across both rural and urban landscapes - the degradation of environmental aesthetics. Whenever I reflect on my childhood in the village, I realise that one of the greatest luxuries we possessed was not electricity, but the enchanting beauty of the night. 

Artificial lighting was almost absent, except for the faint glow of kerosene lamps inside a few houses. After dinner, a handful of people, particularly service holders and educated villagers, would gather near a house to exchange their day’s thoughts. Students quietly studied under kerosene lamps, conscious that fuel was precious, while most families retired early and rose with the dawn. The night belonged to nature, families and quiet reflection. The sky seemed immense, filled with stars; the sounds of crickets, frogs, birds and rustling leaves created a natural symphony. 

There was little incentive to compete with neighbours in displaying wealth. Education, character, hard work and relationships commanded greater respect than extravagance. These memories make me wonder whether, in our pursuit of modernity, we have forgotten the value of darkness itself. Today, the village night is changing rapidly. Powerful floodlights, laser beams, giant LED screens and high-powered loudspeakers can transform social and religious functions into spectacular displays. A celebration that once brought people together can become a public demonstration of prosperity. 

A few decorative lamps may create warmth and beauty; but when hundreds of lights, elaborate structures, extravagant feasts and powerful sound systems are installed primarily to attract attention, consumption acquires another purpose: status signaling. This is what economists describe as conspicuous consumption - spending not merely for usefulness or comfort, but also to demonstrate wealth and social standing. The problem becomes more complicated when positional competition enters the picture. One family’s extravagant celebration becomes another family's benchmark: If they can do this, why can’t we? The next celebration must then be brighter, louder or more elaborate. 

Gradually, expenditure itself becomes a measure of prestige. Whether wealth is earned legitimately or otherwise, conspicuous display can create a social expectation that visible expenditure is a measure of success. The environmental consequences of this competition are rarely considered. As celebrations become more spectacular, natural darkness disappears beneath artificial illumination and the natural soundscape is overwhelmed by amplified music. Stars become difficult to see, sleep is disturbed and the quiet ecological life of the night is disrupted. 

Nocturnal insects, birds, bats and other organisms depend upon darkness and natural rhythms; excessive artificial light and noise can interfere with these relationships. What disappears, therefore, is not simply darkness but an entire environmental experience - the visual beauty of the night, its natural sounds, tranquility and ecological character. There is also a cultural and educational dimension . Traditional village celebrations often reflected local craftsmanship, folk music, earthen lamps and community participation. Increasingly, commercially rented lighting, electronic entertainment and visual extravagance can make one celebration resemble another, gradually weakening local distinctiveness. 

More importantly, children learn from what society admires. If they repeatedly see wealth displayed through spectacular celebrations receiving greater admiration than knowledge, simplicity or service, they may absorb the unfortunate message that success is something to be displayed rather than something to be earned. This should be regarded as a question for serious research rather than an established cause-and-effect conclusion. Perhaps this is why I feel we need to speak about aesthetic pollution - an emerging dimension of environmental degradation in which excessive artificial light, sound and visual clutter diminish the beauty, harmony and sensory character of a place. 

Electricity itself is not the problem; indeed, it is one of the greatest achievements of modern civilisation and an essential foundation for rural development. Reliable electricity has transformed education, healthcare, communication, agriculture, small industries and countless aspects of everyday life. The question is not whether villages should be illuminated, but how much illumination is necessary and where it becomes excessive. Progress should provide light for learning, safety and productive activity not turn every social celebration into a competition of brightness and noise. What we need is not less progress, but more responsible progress that respects both human aspirations and the natural environment. 

I sometimes feel an irresistible urge to stand in the middle of my village and speak aloud - not against electricity, prosperity or celebration, but against our failure to recognise what we are losing. The answer is not to return to a life without electricity, nor to reject progress. It is to learn restraint. A truly beautiful celebration need not conquer the night with dazzling lights and deafening sound. Perhaps the real measure of progress is whether we can celebrate joyfully while leaving the stars visible, the night peaceful, the environment healthy and the minds of our children illuminated by something more enduring than artificial light: knowledge, imagination and wisdom. 

(The writer is former Senior Scientist, Central Pollution Contral Board)

editorials.title: The Mundhe Problem
editorials.passage:
India should not need a celebrity bureaucrat to make the state enforce its own laws. Yet Tukaram Mundhe has become one precisely because, as Maharashtra’s Food and Drug Administration commissioner, he has made enforcement unusually visible. In less than four months, the FDA has dramatically increased inspections and testing, acted against hundreds of food and drug establishments and brought the regulator into places where it was previously easy to assume that nobody was looking. 

The public enthusiasm is understandable. Food and drug safety is not an abstract regulatory concern. Contaminated food can make people ill, damage livelihoods and, on a large scale, impose a substantial economic cost. When an official actually enters kitchens, examines warehouses and acts against violations, citizens see the government doing something tangible. But Mundhe’s popularity also exposes an uncomfortable institutional truth. The extraordinary popularity of an officer doing an ordinary job is evidence that the ordinary system has been performing extraordinarily poorly. 

Mundhe’s reputation did not begin with food safety. An IAS officer since 2005, he has accumulated a reputation for surprise inspections, strict enforcement and an unusually uncompromising administrative style. His career has also been marked by frequent transfers. Supporters regard them as the price of independence; critics see in them a recurring inability to work within institutions and with elected representatives. That debate matters now because food and drug regulation presents a particularly clear test. Enforcement must be tough enough to protect consumers, but predictable enough to protect legitimate businesses from arbitrary administration. 

A regulator cannot confuse severity with effectiveness. Nor can due process become a convenient excuse for doing nothing. Mundhe’s own department has demonstrated both sides of this tension. Its campaign has uncovered serious violations, but courts have also criticised some actions as excessive. The lesson should not be that regulators must retreat. It should be that strong enforcement and due process are not alternatives. A credible regulator needs both. The danger lies in confusing visibility with reform. A raid produces an immediate headline; institutional reform is quieter and slower. The real achievement would be to make compliance routine enough that neither raids nor personalities are required to command public attention. 

There is, however, a more important question. What happens after Mundhe leaves? Maharashtra has now begun moving from spectacular raids towards a more systematic approach to inspections and sampling. That is the direction that matters. If food safety improves only when Mundhe is in the building, Maharashtra has not solved its problem. It has merely found an unusually energetic man to compensate for an unusually weak institution. India needs more regulators willing to act without fear or favour. But it needs fewer regulatory systems dependent on personalities. The ultimate measure of Mundhe’s success will therefore not be his follower count, the number of raids or even the number of licences suspended. It will be whether, after the next transfer, the system keeps doing what Mundhe made it famous for doing.

editorials.title: Meta’s Blind Spot
editorials.passage:
The most disturbing aspect of the latest revelations about child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Meta’s platforms is not that criminals have discovered another way to exploit technology. Criminals will always seek loopholes. The deeper problem is that a company possessing extraordinary technological resources, sophisticated advertising systems and vast amounts of user data appears unable to prevent its platforms from being used to market the sexual exploitation of children. 

This is not an ordinary contentmoderation problem. Advertising is a commercial transaction. An advertisement is created, submitted, reviewed, approved and distributed according to rules established by the platform. If advertisements containing AI-generated sexual abuse imagery can pass through that process repeatedly, the failure extends beyond an imperfect algorithm. It raises questions about the effectiveness of Meta’s system of corporate oversight; some will say about its intentions. 

The government has already ordered Meta to remove material promoting child sexual abuse after earlier investigations exposed the problem. Yet a subsequent investigation reportedly found 84 such advertisements in India, with 78 appearing after the intervention. New examples were also identified after Meta had been alerted to the findings. At that point, “no system is perfect” becomes an unconvincing defence. When the same category of criminal abuse continues to penetrate a system after warnings, regulatory intervention and public scrutiny, the relevant question is whether the company has adequately redesigned that system. AI makes the stakes considerably higher. 

The danger is no longer confined to the circulation of existing abusive material. Artificial intelligence can transform photographs of real children into synthetic sexual imagery and can potentially make the production of such material cheaper, faster and harder to detect. The distinction between “real” and “fake” abuse is therefore morally and legally inadequate. A child whose image is appropriated and sexually manipulated is still being victimised. India must also confront a second question: what happens after platforms detect such material? Reporting to an international child-protection clearing house may satisfy certain obligations, but Indian authorities need the ability to identify offenders operating within India, trace their networks and pursue prosecutions under Indian law. 

Platform cooperation cannot be reduced to removing content after someone else discovers it. The involvement of advertising intermediaries adds another layer of responsibility. If third-party resellers can place billions of dollars of advertising on Meta’s platforms, their activities cannot be treated as someone else’s problem. A company cannot outsource commercial distribution while retaining only nominal responsibility for what enters its advertising ecosystem. 

The larger lesson is uncomfortable. Meta’s enormous scale is often presented as a technological achievement. But scale also creates an obligation to build proportionately serious safeguards. When the victims are children, delayed detection is not merely an operational inconvenience. It can mean that abuse is amplified, monetised and reproduced. The real measure of Meta’s commitment will therefore not be how convincingly it explains each failure. It will be whether the next criminal advertisement is stopped before it reaches an audience.

editorials.title: Goodwill matters
editorials.passage:
It sounded like small fry on Sunday, August 30, 2026, when newspapers reported that a Turkish ferry boat had capsized in the Mediterranean, taking eight passengers — all Turks — to a watery grave. Far greater dangers threatened mankind elsewhere in the world. What made this disaster significant was Greek Cyprus’s immediate offer of helping the enemy with rescue operations.

Despite the standard protocol of exchanging condolences in the face of death, the diatribes that Donald Trump and Iran’s Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei trade almost as a matter of form hardly suggest much scope for cooperation. Yet, the late General Hussain Muhammad Ershad, Bangladesh’s military dictator for most of the 1980s, reportedly became close to Rauf Denktas, the self-proclaimed president of the secessionist Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. Ershad’s Bangladesh didn’t quite offer to apprehend Sylheti migrants in ‘Azad Kashmir’. But it was whispered at one time that he might be the first head of State to extend diplomatic recognition to the breakaway republic. Paradoxically, a Bengali Hindu with ancestral roots in East Bengal had little difficulty in savouring the lost nostalgia of the rebel Turkish entity in a divided Cyprus that has reversed the roles of the protagonists.

No sooner had the tocsin sounded on August 30 than the embodiment of Greek Cypriot legitimacy in the form of President Nikos Christodoulides, head of both State and government, and his foreign minister, Constantinos Kombos, reached out via the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus to convey their readiness to assist the rebel north or even take over relief operations. They were well aware that the ill-fated boat was Turkish-owned and managed, and that it was sailing from Kyrenia in hostile North Cyprus to Tasucu in equally hostile mainland Turkey with Turks on board. But as Nicosia informed the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre, protecting human life being its top priority, it was ready to deploy air and naval search and rescue assets.

If nothing came of this generosity, it may have been because of rumours of the catamaran’s controversial past. Also, Greek Cypriot efforts seemed likely to duplicate the measures taken by the northern maritime and coast guard units as well as mainland Turkey. No one however accused Greek Cypriots of in any way replicating Harry Truman’s dilly-dallying over Jawaharlal Nehru’s 1947 plea for the loan of 10 aircraft to rescue 50,000 Punjabi Hindus who had fled to the North-West Frontier Province and dared not risk the overland journey back after 500 Hindu men, women and children were cut down. Nehru agreed to bear the cost of fuel, oil, maintenance, the crew’s food, quarters and protection but to no avail.

Not that magnanimity has not sometimes raised diplomacy above the level of transactional exchanges. West Asia still remembers that when Richard the Lionheart fell sick during the Crusades, Saladin (Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, the Kurdish commander) sent his own physician to treat the king. When Richard’s horse was killed, Saladin again sent two fresh Arab steeds so that the monarch could continue to do battle on equal terms. No mercy was the code on the battlefield. It was different off the field.

But why look so far? Singapore’s sixth president, Sellappan Rama Nathan, a former head of Intelligence, told an amusing story about the 1965 India-Pakistan war when I was writing Looking East to Look West: Lee Kuan Yew’s Mission India .

When Indian troops captured posts on the Pakistani side of the Line of Control in Kashmir, Ayub Khan retaliated with Operation Grand Slam — an assault using Patton tanks given by the United States of America for defence against the Soviet Union and China — to cut Kashmir off from the rest of India. This was serious stuff, more serious than any skirmish in the mountains, and provoked the major Indian diversionary move of sending troops into Pakistani Punjab so that Lahore came under fire. Pakistan accused India of trying to suppress a revolt by Kashmiri freedom-fighters. But The New York Times reported otherwise: “Reporters who were in Kashmir at the time saw no evidence of an internal rebellion. The … Kashmiris seemed more concerned with selling rugs and renting houseboats to the tourists than in taking up arms for freedom.”

The war ended on September 23 with a United Nations-sponsored ceasefire that settled nothing. Nevertheless, Ayub made a joke of it a year later when Nathan and Sinnathamby Rajaratnam, Singapore’s first and long-time foreign minister of Sri Lankan descent, visited Karachi for an Ecafe (Economic Commission for Asia and the Far East) meeting. Ayub invited the Singaporeans to dinner where Nathan found the Pakistani dictator very Prussian in bearing and manner as he chatted with Singapore’s foreign minister.

“You know we fought a war, Raja? I would call my friend Gary (an imaginary character on the Indian side) and tell him, ‘I am going to have a shower, will you stop the bombardment?’ And Gary would stop the bombardment. And I would have my shower. And Gary (or whoever it was) would call me. ‘Eh Ayub, do you remember our mutual friend so and so? His son has been shot over your territory, look after him.’ I would go there and say, ‘Do you have a boy by this name? He’s my friend’s son. Look after him, will you.’”

“The Prussian image vanished and was replaced by a bluff British soldier as Ayub Khan prattled on merrily, making the war sound like a game of cricket. ‘Very British!’ Nathan laughed, ‘Very, very British!’”

My favourite story of goodwill across battle lines concerns, as these columns have noted before, the Calcutta-born Lieutenant Indra Lal Roy, a World War I flying ace who joined the Royal Flying Corps in Britain in April 1917 when he was just 18 years old. His was a brilliant but tragically brief career for Laddie — as Roy was known in the circle of family and friends — was shot down and killed in a dogfight over France on July 22, 1918. Posthumously awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross, he was buried at Estevelles Communal Cemetery in then German-occupied France. Laddie wasn’t even 20 then. The Bengali inscription on his grave reads, “ Maha birer samadhi; sambhram dekhao, sparsha koro na. ” That translates to: ‘The grave of a courageous warrior; respect it, do not touch it.’

A German fighter dropped a wreath on the grave as the burial was taking place but this was probably the act of an unknown admirer and not the German ace pilot, Manfred von Richthofen, the ‘Red Baron’, as he was nicknamed. But such was the legend of Laddie that many credit the famous Red Baron with the tribute.

Anonymity makes the gesture even more poignant as a pointer to future global cooperation. As this newspaper reported recently, Nepal has been waiting for several years for action on an ambitious Green Climate Fund involving not just massive spending but also specialised research on many fronts dictated by a visionary perception of the future. Meanwhile, Israel attacks West Bank settlements, Trump bombs Iran, and Russia ravages Ukraine.

The Greek Cypriot example is the only way to survival before an Armageddon devours today’s warring states. Applied in the Himalayas, the gesture could not only set a precedent for global cooperation but also help alleviate some of the suffering caused by catastrophic flooding and disastrous earthquakes.

editorials.title: Emily Eden’s art reread
editorials.passage:
A large ship named HMS Jupiter reached Calcutta on March 4, 1836. Hinting at this ‘somehow’ bearable journey from Portsmouth to Calcutta, which took five odd months, one of the passengers commented, “unwelcome ordeal to be endured for a higher purpose”.

The commentator, an elite English woman, was Emily Eden. Along with her sister, Fanny, and their enthusiastic cousin, William Osborne, she had accompanied their brother, George Eden, better known in history as Lord Auckland, whose short but significant political career as the Governor General of India was taking off at the age of 51.

During her time in India, Emily embarked on extensive writing and painting as she tagged along with her brother carrying her sketchbooks. Soon, these would be filled with drawings of princes and commoners alike along with plants, flowers, portraits of the kids of her personal staff and almost everything that appealed to her.

Notably, Emily had been painting when she was in England and she was passionate about her practice. Consequently, when she returned home in 1842, she got 29 of her works published as a series, naming it Portraits of Princes and People of India (1844) .

Almost two centuries later, Emily’s works are being reread with Delhi Art Gallery’s recent landmark show, Princes & People of India: Portraits by Emily Eden , which was themed on her artistic creations. Titled and curated by the cultural and art historian, Mary Ann Prior, also the author of An Indian Portfolio: The Life and Work of Emily Eden , the exhibition featured fantastic originals from the published series of 1844 along with other exhibits like letters, journals from the recently acquired Eden Family Archives, and a rare corpus of Lahore School of Company Paintings for the first time in India.

Beginning late eighteenth century, the art history of the subcontinent was dotted by the presence of painters and writers who wilfully visited India for a unique artistic experience. Early on in the day, the Daniells — uncle and nephew — came and stayed for a couple of years, returning with a huge body of work. This was followed by the arrival of William Hodges (the first professional landscape painter to visit India), George Lambert, Samuel Scott and others.

If this was the trend, then what makes Emily Eden’s visit and oeuvre a talking point?

Emily is perhaps the only English woman who painted and wrote about India simultaneously. Her multistranded creativity presented a distinct and complex experience of the land, what Prior describes as “the most complete record of a very unusual experience, that of travelling across India in the first half of the nineteenth century, meeting the country’s nobility and encountering a vast array of other people, including court attendants, servants, fakirs, farmers and wrestlers.”

While Emily’s contemporaries and forerunners were mostly men who primarily painted stunning ancient, medieval and Mughal architecture, Emily painted people, both the nobility and the commoner, with the same gusto. It is Emily’s gender-driven perspective and her anthropological interests in various communities of India that make her art distinct. To this one must add her ‘greater purpose’: a ‘purpose’ that twinned the ‘political’ with the ‘personal’. Her visit to India was driven by her unflinching support for her brother, George. George’s political mobility and position in the East India Company mattered to her, even if that meant a low profile for herself. Prior notes that “Without the help of Emily and her sister, Fanny, George would not have been able to achieve high office.”

The East India Company needed allies to counter Russian power in Central Asia and George Eden’s primary task was to check Tsar Nicholas I’s military advances into British-Indian territory through the Northwest’s border provinces. By the 1830s, the Russians had been trying to capture Herat, a strategically located Afghan city. The urgent need to find potential allies compelled George to take a trip of around 1,700 kilometres from Calcutta to Lahore with the intent to meet and negotiate with Maharaja Ranjit Singh who could help the British in checking Russian moves. The two-year-long trip consisted of a huge entourage of men, women and children — no less than 12,000 — travelling through Benares, Patna, Delhi, Gwalior, Lucknow, Patiala, Amritsar, Allahabad and Shimla, before they reached their destination.

On their way, they stopped by at several princely kingdoms, being hosted as official guests, like in Patiala, Punjab. As a gesture of reciprocation, Emily began drawing portraits; in this instance of Raja Karam Singh, the ruler of Patiala. What is worth noticing is the access that Emily got into Indian princely families which enabled a deeper engagement. The art that developed out of such engagements was a component of soft, cultural diplomacy, which she would then continue throughout.

However, this approach is best reflected by her engagements with Maharaja Ranjit Singh and his family in Lahore.

When the entourage reached Lahore in 1838, George and East India Company officials got busy in negotiating what would be in the best interest of the Company while Emily missed no opportunity to acquaint with the royals. The Sikh ruler, who was known for not accommodating artists, was persuaded by Emily for more than one sitting even though his health was in decline. On the other hand, the Edens were treated very well, so much so that they decided to spend their Christmas as royal guests in Lahore. Seemingly, Emily was sought after as a portrait artist, with the Indian nobility wanting to have their portraits made by an English artist and an elite lady at that.

Other than her portraits of Ranjit Singh, Emily also painted a family portrait of Dost Mohammad, the Afghan amir who visited the Edens at the Government House in Calcutta and was very much part of the British political alliances. The portraits do add up to George’s political imaging and serve as more than souvenirs from the empire even though they limit Emily’s artistry to ‘only imprints of cultural diplomacy’. By way of their artistic brilliance, they stand out as significant artworks from the colonial era.

But what makes Emily’s work significant is her deep anthropological interest in India. Looking at them, one can sense her curious mind, read into a persona which never failed to grab a chance to make sketches of the people of this country right from the day she had sketched a student studying at the Hindu College, Calcutta.

Emily Eden’s works have become a valuable anthropological record that had not only served the empire but also opened a gateway of interest for post-colonial and feminist scholarship or for anyone willing to deconstruct her striking compositions. The only other English woman who has had such close encounters with India is Fanny Parks, but that’s another story.

Nilosree Biswas is an author, columnist and film-maker

editorials.title: Terror’s long shadow: Editorial on the lasting legacy of 9/11 and the era of fear
editorials.passage:
In a world that is continuously changing, few events stand out as particularly transformative — life looked very different before and after them. September 11, 2001 was one such day. Twenty-five years ago, nearly 3,000 people died in the United States of America on that day after terrorists flew jetliners into the Twin Towers in New York and the Pentagon outside Washington D.C.; another plane crash-landed after passengers tried to wrest control of the flight from the hijackers. To Americans, this was a moment similar to the horror called Pearl Harbour. But September 11 shook the whole world and left an impact on it in ways which the Japanese attack in December 1941 never did. A so-called war on terror was launched. Air travel would never look the same again. The balance between the rights of citizens and the powers of security agencies shifted definitively — in favour of the latter. A spate of invasions and conflicts followed, bringing more death and devastation. International law took a hit. Existing religious fissures deepened across the world, amplifying hate and bigotry. Most significantly, 9/11 led to the inception of an era of fear that has lingered.

The distrust and divisions are on display even 25 years after the terrorist attacks. Last year, New York City elected its first Muslim mayor, Zohran Mamdani. But his religious identity also set off calls by some, including Rudy Giuliani — who was mayor on September 11 — for Mr Mamdani to not be allowed at the memorial for victims. The attacks in 2001 inspired terrorist groups and led to a surge in Islamophobia; hate crimes against Muslims and those thought to be Muslims surged across the world. The US invaded Afghanistan and, then, two years later — without the United Nations’ approval — Iraq. Yet it found Osama bin Laden, the architect of the September 11 attacks, in Pakistan, a country Washington treated as an ally. The wars decimated al Qaida, the group behind the September 11 attacks but also spawned new outfits like the Islamic State. A new language also emerged out of the fumes of conflicts. Phrases like ‘collateral damage’, ‘axis of evil’, ‘enhanced interrogation’ and ‘extraordinary rendition’ were used to sanitise the killings of civilians, torture, the incarceration of prisoners without due process, and the dehumanisation of entire polities perceived by the US as its enemies. Civil liberties were weakened, as the US and other countries around the world justified spying on civilians and conceiving stringent anti-terror laws in the name of security. And while the US was ground zero of the terror attack, countless people died from the retaliatory wars that followed in countries covering a wide geographical span.

There is a line of thought that suggests that the clearest proof of the lasting legacy of September 11 lies in the present era of endless wars. It cites the fire of Russian aggression in Ukraine and the US’s military intervention in Iran as cases in point. The Global Peace Index had estimated in 2024 that the number of wars being fought around the globe has been the highest since World War II. But 9/11 can be viewed in another — important — way. It ushered in a sense of perpetual fear — within nations, among collectives, and even inside the mind — that persists. The global fraternity must ponder this fear, and ways to exorcise it, urgently.

editorials.title: Climate: Time for BRICS to act
editorials.passage:
Let’s begin with a number that should end the debate before it starts: $170 billion. That is the annual climate finance gap developing countries face, the difference between what they need to adapt to a crisis they did not create, and what the Global North has actually delivered.

At COP29, the much-celebrated climate finance deal committed $300 billion annually by 2035, a figure that the very nations it was meant to serve called “disappointingly low” and “an insult”. India’s chief negotiator walked out. The Global South’s patience, already wearing dangerously thin, is now effectively exhausted.

Into this vacuum steps the most consequential geopolitical bloc the climate world has yet to fully reckon with: BRICS.

BRICS is no longer the acronym of a Goldman Sachs investment thesis. It is a 45-member-strong economic coalition — following the 2024 expansion; representing over 40 per cent of global GDP, more than 50 per cent of the world’s population, and crucially, the majority of the world’s most climate-exposed communities.

Brazil’s Amazon is the planet’s most critical carbon sink. Russia’s permafrost holds one of its largest methane time bombs. India has crossed 52 per cent non-fossil electricity capacity and is racing towards 500 gigawatts of renewables.

China is manufacturing 80 per cent of the world’s solar panels. South Africa sits at the heart of the continent that is losing the most while contributing the least to the crisis. This is not a bloc on the periphery of the climate conversation. It is the conversation.

And yet BRICS has spent the better part of the last decade deferring to a Global North climate architecture that has consistently failed it — promising technology transfer while patenting it, pledging climate finance while disbursing a fraction of it, and designing adaptation frameworks in Geneva for communities whose names they cannot pronounce.

The recent catastrophic floods in Nepal —submerging entire valleys, displacing hundreds of thousands, and wiping out decades of development gains in 72 hours — are a case study in precisely what happens when the world’s most vulnerable communities are left waiting for a multilateral system that moves at the speed of diplomatic courtesy.

Technologies like that of Climate Risk Observatory — has been generating district and ward-level compound climate risk intelligence for cities across South Asia, including flood, heat, and landslide compound hazard mapping. The technology exists. The methodology exists. The need is screaming. What is missing is the political architecture to deploy it at speed and at scale — and BRICS is uniquely positioned to build that architecture.

Consider what a genuine BRICS Climate Hub would actually look like in practice. The New Development Bank, BRICS’s own multilateral financial institution, already has climate infrastructure lending in its mandate.

What it needs is a Climate Readiness Facility that replicates, for the Global South, what the Green Climate Fund was always supposed to be but never quite became: a fast-disbursing, directly accessible, nationally embedded climate finance instrument that does not require a developing country to spend three years navigating accreditation bureaucracy before its most vulnerable citizens receive a single rupee or rand or real of adaptation support.

The technology transfer question is where the Global North’s credibility collapses most visibly. For 30 years, developed countries have promised to share the clean technologies that make the low-carbon transition possible — and for 30 years, intellectual property regimes have ensured that promise was structurally unfulfillable.

BRICS can break this cycle not by negotiating with the Global North for permission, but by building its own technology commons. China’s solar manufacturing cost curve — which has driven the price of photovoltaic panels down by 90 per cent since 2010 — is the single most important climate technology contribution of the 21st century, and it happened entirely outside the Global North’s technology transfer framework.

India’s green hydrogen mission, Brazil’s sustainable aviation fuel programme, and South Africa’s just transition partnership are all examples of the Global South generating climate solutions at scale. What they need is the institutional architecture to share them with each other — and with Nepal, with Mozambique, with Vietnam — at the speed the climate emergency demands.

The green jobs opportunity is where the BRICS Climate Hub argument becomes not just morally compelling but economically irresistible. India alone has the potential to generate 35 million green jobs by 2047.

Brazil’s bioeconomy could employ 20 million in sustainable agriculture, forest restoration, and green manufacturing by 2035. A coordinated BRICS green jobs compact — linking skills recognition, labour mobility, and green manufacturing investment across member states — would be the largest deliberate employment programme in human history. This is the growth agenda the Global South has been waiting for someone to articulate loudly enough.

For over a decade, Indian climate-focused organisations have worked at the intersection of climate science, institutional governance, and development finance across South Asia and Africa. From pioneering tools such as the Climate Readiness Index and the Mumbai Multi-Hazard Risk Atlas to supporting India’s first Model Heat Action Plan, this journey has been anchored in a fundamental conviction: the Global South must build and own the knowledge, institutions, and financing solutions needed to shape its climate-resilient future — on its own terms, responsive to its realities, and at the pace its people need. Neither can BRICS. The moment is here. The bloc is assembled. The crisis is accelerating. BRICS does not need to become the world’s climate leader by displacing anyone.

It needs to stop stepping aside for institutions that have repeatedly proven they are not equal to the scale of what this moment demands — and start building the architecture, the finance, the technology commons, and the political will to lead from where the crisis is actually being felt.

BRICS: stop waiting. Start building.

Mohanty is Director and Global Sector Head of Climate Change and Sustainability; Singh is Founder and Managing Director- at IPE Global

Published on September 12, 2026

editorials.title: Adapting cooling policy to India’s AI ambitions
editorials.passage:
India is leaping forward as a major hub for artificial intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure. IndiaAI Mission coupled with global technology firms’ investments are facilitating expansion of hyperscale data centers which promises significant economic and technological benefits. However, it raises a parallel policy challenge: cooling. These data centers generate enormous amounts of heat due to the computational intensity of modern AI chips, making cooling systems a major driver of electricity consumption. As India expands its AI infrastructure, the country’s cooling policy, particularly the India Cooling Action Plan (ICAP) must link up cooling requirements of AI.

The total data centre capacity in the country is expected to reach more than 12 GW by 2030 from around 1.5 GW in 2025, and thereby occupying roughly 26.3 GW of electricity consumption by 2031–32 (about 6.7 percent of India’s projected total electricity consumption). Beyond electricity consumption, AI infrastructure has substantial cooling requirements.

High-performance GPUs used for training and deploying AI models operate at extremely high-power densities, generating significant heat that must be removed continuously to maintain system reliability. Cooling systems therefore represent one of the largest energy costs for data centers globally, often accounting for 30–50 percent of total energy consumption. The industry is adopting advanced cooling technologies such as direct-to-chip liquid cooling, adiabatic cooling and immersion cooling to minimise water usage, however usage of fresh water for cooling is there to stay.

India’s Cooling Action Plan introduced in 2019 provided a 20-year roadmap for sustainable cooling across sectors including buildings, cold chains, refrigeration, and transport. It sets ambitious targets to reduce cooling demand by 20–25 percent and cooling energy requirements by 25–40 percent by 2037–38 through improved energy efficiency, better refrigerants, and technological innovation. ICAP represents one of the world’s most comprehensive national cooling strategies and reflects India’s commitment to climate-sensitive infrastructure planning.

However, the rapid rise of AI computing has raised contention of being a stakeholder. When ICAP was formulated, hyperscale AI infrastructure had not yet become a central component of the digital economy. As a result, AI was not part of ICAP framework and it remained focused on conventional cooling applications—such as air conditioning in buildings and refrigeration in supply chains. But now data centers are knocking hard and fast on the door to get a representation in cooling action plans.

Recent discussions at the India AI Impact Summit 2026 underscored the scale of the transformation underway. The summit emphasized that AI is not only a technological revolution but also an infrastructure challenge involving computing power, energy systems, and environmental sustainability. Policymakers highlighted the need for AI development to align with broader climate goals under a framework anchored in “People, Planet, and Progress.” The summit also emphasized the importance of building responsible and sustainable AI ecosystems that can support economic growth while safeguarding environmental resources.

The environmental implications of AI infrastructure extend beyond electricity consumption. Many cooling systems rely heavily on water for heat dissipation, raising concerns in regions already facing water stress. As India’s data-centre sector expands, the energy-water nexus associated with cooling will become an increasingly important policy issue. The rapid growth of AI infrastructure could exacerbate local resource pressures, particularly in urban regions where both electricity demand and water scarcity are already significant challenges.

The principles embedded in ICAP provide a useful starting point for addressing the cooling needs of AI infrastructure. The plan promotes energy-efficient cooling technologies, improved building design, and environmentally sustainable refrigerants. These principles can be extended to data-center operations through the adoption of advanced cooling systems such as liquid cooling, immersion cooling, and heat-recovery technologies. Such innovations are particularly well suited to AI workloads because they can remove heat more efficiently than traditional air-based cooling systems.

Future iterations of cooling strategy should explicitly recognize hyperscale data centers as a distinct sector within ICAP. Establishing performance benchmarks, such as standards for Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and cooling efficiency, would encourage the development of energy-efficient AI infrastructure while reducing the environmental footprint of digital expansion.

In essence the achievement of present ICAP targets can crowd in cooling demand of large AI data centres to put a ceiling on overall cooling requirements in the economy. Going a level ahead, it is also important to optimize the cooling requirements across states. The ICAP has already been implemented across 250 cities in India, which if linked with geographic planning for locating AI centers, offers an opportunity to solve this objective function.

India is a diversified economy with each of its regions bestowed with specific resources. It is high time to tap this potential effectively for AI infrastructure deployment. We have States like Gujarat and Rajasthan where land for renewable resources generation like solar power are enormously available. Similarly, there are few north eastern states and southern ones which have abundant water resource. Technology should also be built in to efficiently use these resources. For example, water quality could be of different grades, the average graded one could be roped in for cooling purpose. Here, case studies of few developed economies like Singapore are an eyeopener.

Banka is Deputy Director; Karthikeyan is Director in Government of India. Views expressed are personal

editorials.title: A knock at democracy’s door
editorials.passage: Nowadays, many political organisations are laying stress on listening to Gen Z youths. Their campaigns themed around the idea of listening, whether they are dubbed samvad (dialogue) or goonj (echoes), are essentially outreach initiatives. However, listening genuinely to agitating youths requires a sensitive understanding of the changing modes of protest in recent times. Protests are usually conceived as a form of posturing that reflects public anger, through various aggressive and, at times, violent means. The recent youth protests are also reminiscent of the “young angry man” archetype. That image, conveying the anger of youths, turned into a popular perception thanks to a trend of Hindi movies in the 1970s. Prior to that, British literature in the 1950s and several labour, student, and youth movements in the ’60s and ’70s prepared the canvas for the depiction of the young angry man in India’s popular culture. Mix of contradictory emotions There is a popular perception that protest is possible merely through aggression and violent anger. But, especially in post-90s India, the popular psyche began to reflect expressions of protest in multiple forms. Besides, over time, the expressions combined many contradictory and overlapping bhavas (feelings), such as anger with joy and laughter, complaints with satire, agitation with carnival, and aggression with reels. A good example of it was observed in the Gen Z movements over education in Jantar Mantar, Jharkhand, and elsewhere in the country. They ruptured a conventional notion of protest where anger, aggression, or even violence is predominant. The contradictory mix of feelings and actions in the protest movements also contributed to a profusion of virtual culture material. If we look back at the biggest student-led movements in the past, including the ones that erupted around the time of Emergency, a display blending binary forms and feelings was rare. Earlier, protests mostly channelled anger and violent acts such as damaging trains or public property and laying siege to official residences. That said, such mixing or mishmash in protest movements are not new but have been practised in various parts of the world for ages. Literary critic and philosopher Mikhail Bakhtin (Rabelais and His World) and anthropologist James C Scott (Weapons of the Weak) have shown in their works how protest actions used laughter, parody, mimicry, and mockery in medieval festivals in European societies. The use of masks, satirical reels, laughter, parody, and celebrative postures by students in India became one of their distinctive features this year. They are, however, identified as pre-political forms of dissent. Pre-political to political: Question of longevity and fragility It is true that Gen Z and even Gen Alpha movements have had success in creating pressure on the government. But questions arise as to whether such agitations, laden with pre-political elements, have the capacity to become political? What is the future of such movements? Can they evolve into a long-term transformative movement in India? One observation is that they mostly are assertions demanding urgent, immediate solutions to specific problems. As a result, they appear reformative in their nature and lack transformative qualities. Any pressure group, as desired by Cockroach Janta Party Founder Abhijit Dipke, to reform the system may not be able to sustain itself without a long-term vision. Secondly, their heavy reliance on pre-political forms of protests certainly helps in spreading awareness but that may not translate into an organised movement. Scholars identify these modes of dissent as short-term and transitory, lacking in longevity. Thirdly, as of now such protests are scattered and dispersed across various parts of India. They are emanating from immediate concerns such as exam paper leaks and sanctity of employment-centred exams and competitions. If the administrative system responds well to the immediate demands, the movements may die out. Political parties that are in the opposition, such as the Congress, may try to give them some life in order to achieve their own political goals. But it is difficult to say whether they will succeed in sustaining them for long. The protests are driven by social media which, by its very nature, generates an impact on the public psyche that is immediate, rapidly changing, fractured, and fragile. Many fragments, one whole It is true that as a cohort Gen Z has a similar mindset, but it is equally true that in India we have multiple Gen Zs. Whether youths who are part of diverse categories such as caste, class, religion, region, urban, and rural may continue to identify with one uniform grouping at the national level for long is debatable. They have their own issues that are local and regional, and political parties and social groups also largely cater to Gen Z constituencies of their own. The access of these groups to students and youths may split a generation in one way or another. It must be said that bringing multiple fragments to form one whole is possible but difficult in the long run in a diverse society like India. Social media and other forms of media are also able to raise local concerns as national ones, yet such a transformation — from the digital and virtual to the physical arena — may not materialise consistently. There is also a question mark about the ability of these protests to build an alternative politics in India. Our democratic politics is flexible and vibrant, full of adaptability and with a capacity of co-opt. There is always a possibility of student leaders joining mainstream political parties or forming new outfits, much like the Aam Aadmi Party was borne out of a movement against corruption. Nevertheless, in their incipient forms, these protests have knocked hard on the door of democracy. That might just compel the governance system and administration at various levels to become more sensitive and inclusive. editorials.title: Securing our skies on our terms
editorials.passage: India’s defence technology modernisation has arrived at a critical geopolitical crossroads. For decades, our security discourse was shackled to a restrictive, transactional matrix: Outright procurement, licensed assembly, and the familiar promises of the so-called “transfer of technology” (ToT). While these mechanisms may have met the immediate operational needs of a previous era, they are entirely insufficient for a nation asserting its place as an unyielding global power. The definitive question for our defence planners is no longer what technology platforms India can buy, but when a multi-billion-dollar defence contract concludes, what permanent technological capabilities are left behind on Indian soil for us to carry forward. This paradigm shift must even dictate our execution of the flagship Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme. Public debate around this fifth-generation fighter heavily obsesses over production timelines, thrust-to-weight ratios, and short-term capital allocations. However, the true national dividend of the AMCA project lies not simply in the stealth fighters rolling off the assembly line, but in the comprehensive, independent industrial architecture we build around it. ALSO READBuilding India’s REITs True aerospace sovereignty cannot be imported in a crate. Historically, nations that have sustained a dominant combat aviation edge did not do so via isolated, transactional purchases. They built a sprawling domestic web of advanced engineering talent, sovereign airworthiness certification authorities, complex testing infrastructures, and an industrial base of precision suppliers. These networks are genuine national assets and foundational structures designed to birth successive generations of home-grown platforms. Conventional outright buys or conventional ToT models have frequently acted as gilded cages. To shatter this cycle, the AMCA programme can be an example to demonstrate as a nation-building catalyst. Indian industry must rapidly graduate from being a low-tier assembly destination to an independent hub of design authority and precision engineering. Achieving true resilience demands the systematic cultivation of a local supplier ecosystem capable of manufacturing high-tolerance spares and precision-engineered sub-systems. India needs a formidable network of private and public technology champions who can match global aerospace standards while keeping the intellectual and physical capital anchored at home. This requires an aggressive, targeted focus on the building blocks of modern military propulsion. Precision machining ecosystems are a huge area for Indian defence tech startups and MSMEs capable of manufacturing complex sub-components down to sub-micron tolerances. ALSO READElectricity, not oil, should define growth Establishing local foundry capabilities for specialised super alloys and complex advanced coatings is a must. Ensure that the entire spare part loop, from initial digital design to casting, is completely insulated from external sanctions or regional geopolitical pressures. By establishing this structural depth, India can transition from a net consumer of aerospace parts to an independent global node in advanced manufacturing. This domestic industrial revolution requires a clean break from conventional international partnerships. As India evaluates strategic options for the AMCA-Mk2 engine, the benchmark must look past immediate technology access. The most valuable alliances are those that treat India not as a captive consumer market, but as an equal co-development hub. Consider the immense strategic advantage of aligning with an engine partner uniquely prepared to co-create a dedicated, sovereign aero gas-turbine complex inside India. The ideal collaborator is one that moves away from modified legacy engines and instead offers a clean-sheet, next-generation engine designed, engineered, and manufactured from scratch on Indian soil. The ultimate differentiator in this model is the total relinquishment of intellectual property (IP) barriers. When a partner offers joint ownership of core IP, they hand India the keys to the propulsion kingdom. This gives our scientists and engineers the absolute freedom to modify, scale, and upgrade the engine architecture for future sixth-generation platforms or naval variants without seeking permission from foreign boards or capitals. Furthermore, this model directly unlocks the most fiercely guarded frontiers of metallurgy. True collaboration means mastering the capability to mass-produce single-crystal turbine blades and advanced thermal barrier coatings locally. Cultivating the specialised knowledge to cast a turbine blade as a single, flawless crystal capable of operating under immense centrifugal forces and temperatures exceeding is precisely what transforms India from a buyer to an aerospace peer. The history of leading aerospace nations proves that advanced propulsion cannot be achieved through shortcuts; it is an incremental journey built across generations. By entering a co-development architecture that guarantees full IP rights and domestic manufacturing depth, India can leapfrog decades of trial and error. The legacy of the AMCA project must not be a fleet of advanced aircraft reliant on foreign lifelines for propulsion and spares. Its ultimate triumph must be the creation of a sophisticated domestic engineering ecosystem, unmatched industrial depth, and the strategic resilience needed to secure our skies on our own terms. That is the true definition of a self-reliant India and it is an opportunity we must boldly claim. The OEMs willing to go on these parameters and co-developing as well as collaborating to produce precision engineering and components should be given preferential access whether in defence tech or even civilian purchases, including passenger civilian planes. India needs to shift the benchmark from a passive transfer of technology to a true peer-level partnership that is sanction-proof and builds local capabilities in parallel. India then stops being a captive destination for assembly and transforms into a global power centre for advanced propulsion design.
