editorials.title: ‘Goa has become internally exotic in India because of its Portuguese heritage’
editorials.passage:
Goans have moved across continents for centuries, travelling as Portuguese nationals through British colonies, building communities in East Africa, navigating citizenship regimes that could not decide whether they were Indian, European, or something else entirely. R Benedito Ferrão’s Across Continents: Writing Goans, Making Worlds examines what happens when that experience enters fiction. Published in Michigan University Press’s African Perspectives series, the book reads Goan characters across four novels connected to different continents: Salman Rushdie’s Midnight’s Children , MG Vassanji’s The Book of Secrets , Roger King’s A Girl from Zanzibar , and Margaret Mascarenhas’s Skin , bringing paintings, etchings, and pop music into dialogue with the literary texts to surface what prose alone leaves buried.

Ferrão is an Associate Professor of English and Asian and Pacific Islander American Studies at William & Mary, Virginia, US. Additionally, he is the Dr Thomas Tam Visiting Professor of Asian American Studies at the City University of New York’s Asian American/Asian Research Institute. His previous publications include the edited volume Goa, Portugal, Mozambique: The Many Lives of Vamona Navelcar , which accompanied an exhibition he curated at Fundação Oriente in Goa, and the co-published The Girl Who was the Color of Nothing: A Children’s Story for Adults with the artist, Maria Vanessa de Sa, who also created the cover image for Across Continents .

In this conversation with Scroll , Ferrão discussed the personal roots of his monograph, why Portuguese colonialism demands its own critical vocabulary, and what comes next for the study of Goan diasporic literature.

Across Continents opens with a series of autobiographical moments: your grandparents’ journey from Portuguese Goa to British East Africa, a trip to a Mombasa cemetery to find the grave of your maternal grandmother, Felicidade, and the story of a family friend, Mr M, who turned out to be a Black Mozambican man married to a Goan woman with adopted children from a local orphanage. You write that “Mr M and his family, as well as Felicidade, could well have been characters in the kinds of novels I came to research.” In the acknowledgements, you describe the book as having been sparked by a conversation “in a moment of crisis” in Sharjah with the editors of the African Perspectives series at University of Michigan Press. What is the relationship between these personal histories and the scholarly argument that follows? At what point did you recognise that the family story and the academic project were the same story? “Where are you from?” As someone who has moved a fair bit in their life, this question is a constant. It seems unusual to those making this query that my response is never just the one place prior. This was never something extraordinary to me given my family history as you have remarked upon; yet, such displacement was also not something I understood to be specific to my family alone, given that it was a commonplace story among many Goans I encountered.

While I knew from a young age that my family had an African history, what was less apparent to me was Goa’s own African heritage. Even so, someone like Mr M was not an aberration, although Blackness in Goa is a subject that causes unease (as I touch upon in Across Continents ).

The explanation for the occurrences of both these instances of diaspora – the Goan presence in Africa and the African presence in Goa – may be found in the humanistic social sciences and even in historical evidence. Among other reasons are changes in Goa’s agrarian economy, as well as the transcontinental relations between the Portuguese and British empires. What these fields of study are unable to account for, nonetheless, are the affective lives of ordinary diasporic subjects. How did ambition, loss, and love factor into their lived experience? What did it mean to leave a familiar land behind, remake home in a new continent, and then be exiled to yet another foreign place? I turned to literature to gather some semblance of answers to these questions. And while fiction is exactly that, it still gives reality a shape, especially when the unrecorded past is something we can only know by approximation.

I hasten to add that in studying the literature I did, it was not “to find myself.” Instead, I wanted to understand how fiction with a historical basis portrays the displacement of minority subjects – notably the kind whose movements are impelled by political events. And perhaps that is where the personal and the academic converge for me in helping me query the relationship of the nation to the individual. This, not least, when the person does not seem to belong properly to any one place, thereby querying the conceptual limits of nationality and citizenship.

“Where are you from?” is a question that should be regarded suspiciously. It implies that the “where” is not “here” and that the subject will and must return to that foreign place from whence they sprung. The question is most chilling when asked of you by an official as you seek entry into the country of your residence. What is to be made of the person whose familial “origins” truly cannot be consigned to just one location?

As you underscore, the genesis of this book was a conversation that occurred in Sharjah, which by happenstance is in the region of the country where I was born. And this geographic coincidence is germane to the publication of this monograph because the crisis that occasioned the conversation with the editors of the series in which it finally found its home had to do with the book not fitting neatly into the usual disciplinary categories, much like Goan identity and its representation. At once a work that relates to African, Asian, Asian American, and Indian Ocean literatures, this book is also not specific to any of those classifications, stretching – as the title indicates – multicontinentally.

One of the book’s central claims is that postcolonial literary studies has a structural blind spot when it comes to Portuguese colonialism. You introduce the term “lusosphere” in preference to “lusophone,” arguing that it “allows for an understanding of Portuguese colonialism and cultural development that is not connected only to language.” This reframing runs through the entire book, from the introduction’s observation that Goan identity has been “malleable, lacking fixity” since the Pombaline reforms of the eighteenth century, through to the concluding chapter’s insistence that the Indian and Atlantic Oceans cannot be treated as discrete systems. How did you arrive at this term, and how has the argument that Portuguese colonialism requires its own critical vocabulary been received by scholars working within established postcolonial frameworks? Even the Marquis de Pombal (1699-1782; in office, 1750-1777) was influenced in his political ideas by his time outside Portugal; he had served as the ambassador to England. Indeed, the form of Portuguese citizenship that Goans still have birthright access to, even presently, arose in large part because the Portuguese empire was diminishing in power in relation to the ascendancy of its British counterpart.

Unlike those in the British Empire, people in Portugal’s overseas territories were considered citizens rather than subjects. To be clear, this was not a move towards racial equality. Because Portuguese imperial supremacy waned so rapidly following their initial early modern conquest of Goa, extending citizenship rights to those beyond the metropole was an expedient move in maintaining empire from afar, as it could involve the colonised as compradors and in self-preservation.

Of course, this meant that it was not only the elite who fell under the umbrella of Portuguese citizenship. Subalterns who may not have had great facility in the Portuguese language were nonetheless still Portuguese and could use their citizenship privileges to remove themselves from the caste and class conscriptions in Goa which could pin them to an unchanging existence. This then meant that several Goans travelled between Portuguese India and British India and, thereafter, to British and Portuguese Africas to change their lot in life. Even as some of these diasporic subjects may not have been lusophone, the expansive array of transcontinental and transoceanic locations they traversed constitutes the lusosphere – an ambit made possible by Portuguese colonialism, culture, and its remaking. Evidence of such displacements emerges in the texts I write about.

Postcolonial studies continues to have an unacknowledged Anglocentric bias. The reason this does not work in understanding lusospheric contexts has much to do with the durée of Portuguese rule in South Asia and elsewhere being far greater than that of the British presence. This is an observation also made by the historians Rochelle Pinto and Anjali Arondekar . The movements of Goan diasporic subjects represented literarily challenge postcolonialists, especially because a one-size-fits-all approach does not work in explaining how such figures manoeuvred between colonialities as non-white Europeans.

Midnight’s Children is one of the most extensively analysed postcolonial novels in existence. Although this is true, no one had adequately analysed it from the angle of Portuguese colonialism, Goan history, and the novel’s disconnection from Africa. Further, you mention a Goan poet who had begun and then abandoned a novel about a child born at the exact moment of independence, not in Bombay but in Goa. You write that “one can only speculate the reasons for which the unnamed Goan poet gave up the task of completing a story so similar to, and dreamed up within the same chronological moment as, Rushdie’s.” What made you decide to take on a text with such a vast critical literature, and what does that abandoned Goan novel tell us about the relationship between Goan literary production and the anglophone canon? This is a wonderful question. In the two Rushdie novels I write about, Midnight’s Children and The Moor’s Last Sigh , I noticed his desire to think about Indo-Portuguese history but then his inability to sustain representation of such alternate South Asian legacies before returning once more to the safety of imagining India as a primarily post-British nation.

A case in point is that the saga of the da Gama-Zogoiby clan of The Moor’s Last Sigh may begin in “exotic” Jewish and Portuguese Cochin but then, quickly, the family moves to what Prema Rocha calls Rushdie’s “beloved metropolis” – the ever-familiar city of Bombay. Now, as we are shown in Midnight’s Children , the author is very aware of even that city’s Portuguese heritage. Yet, Rushdie’s employ of lusospheric heritage is generally in the service of demonstrating the diversity of a Bombay that is part of a British postcoloniality. The exodus of his Mary Pereira-Braganza character, whom I underscore as the lynchpin of the novel’s plot, absents her from the tale once her service is provided as local colour.

The other part of your question, to me, is really about how the nation and its culture relate to the marginalised. As Pamila Gupta and Vishvesh Prabhakar Kandolkar have both argued, Goa has become an “internal exotic” to India because of its Portuguese heritage (and, really, this is proven quite true by how Indian tourism, film, and real estate industries have capitalised on that concept). Now, if exoticism is a dish to be delighted in not by the exotic themselves, then there needs to be a marked difference between the two. In spite of the fact that Goans traversed both Indias and even self-represented their negotiations of these polities since the 19th century in print culture, as Rochelle Pinto catalogues for us in Between Empires , in the post-British Indian imagination, Portuguese India and its heritage have become consumable reappropriations via anglophone representation.

The book’s signature figure is what you call “the postnational Goan,” the character whose identity exceeds every nation-state that attempts to contain it. Your introduction recovers a striking piece of primary evidence: a 1976 House of Lords debate in which peers struggled to categorise newly arrived Goan refugees, with Baroness Llewelyn-Davies declaring “My Lords, there is no Goan citizenship.” And you trace the concept back to an antithesis expressed by the anticolonialist Tristão de Bragança Cunha , who in 1944 declared that “no people is so denationalised as Goans.” How do you distinguish the postnational Goan from the more familiar figure of the transnational migrant in diaspora studies? Is postnationality a condition specific to Goans, or does the book propose it as a model applicable to other communities shaped by overlapping colonial systems? The transnational migrant is a product of neoliberal globali s ation, a worker whose services are attracted and repelled by the forces of political economy that are no longer nationally specific. In contrast, the postnational Goan is an older figure, one with some degree of personal and political agency who navigates multiple cultures and economies.

From the 19th century, Goans reacted to the declining economy in Estado da Índia by using their Portuguese citizenship status to travel transimperially and even transcontinentally. While elite Goans may seem to have been the ones favoured most highly in seeing themselves through these developments, it must be said that subaltern Goans also navigated these volatile conditions with varying degrees of success.

Essentially, Goans parlayed their status as Europeans as a ticket to opportunities elsewhere. These postnationals journeyed as citizens of a country they did not live in to work in some other nation to which they held no immediate allegiance while having emotional and political ties to other lands on more than one continent. This apart, the outsider status of Goans was not always to their advantage, as can be seen in the novels studied in Across Continents . In reality, as in fiction, the Goan has certainly been in excess of nation, something even true today in India where this community has access to Portuguese citizenship but is told that dual citizenship is an impossibility!

As you surmise, no, my theorisation of postnational identity is not exclusively about Goans, although their circumstances are historically quite specific. Rather, it invites us to ask how different kinds of colonialisms have operated in comparison, contest, and conjunction with one another, thereby breaking away from an anglocentric model of postcolonial studies. It also asks us to think about how we can form other conceptions of identity when we are not beholden to the idea of the nation as the only way to conceive of belonging.

The book’s methodology is distinctively intermedial. You read Angelo da Fonseca’s indigenised Catholic iconography alongside Rushdie’s “Blue Jesus” episode, where a priest insists that “Our Lord Christ Jesus was the most beauteous crystal shade of pale sky blue.” You trace Wenceslaus Hollar’s etchings of Tangier alongside the marriage of Catherine of Braganza, and you read Karishma D’Souza’s painting Going Home , which you describe as deriving from “suppressed and unknown family histories of Blackness in Goa,” alongside the slave-trade histories in Mascarenhas’s Skin . How did you arrive at the intermedial method, and what can a painting or an etching reveal about a novel that the text alone cannot? An intermedial method of literary criticism speaks to the multisensory way that the world unfolds before us and how we experience it, even when reading. Looking at a painting, likewise, is a haptic encounter – our sight “touches” the textures of the image and gauges the depth of its composition. So also, to read about Blue Jesus beckons us to imagine an azure-shaded icon, which then has us consider the symbolism of colour and interpretations of faith and devotion.

Across Continents relies on the creativity of such Goan artists as Maria Vanessa de Sa , Karishma D’Souza , Angelo da Fonseca , and others because art is as much an analysis of history as other forms of cultural production, all of them working together to inform our understanding of a historical juncture or event. My Fonsecan reading of Rushdie’s Blue Jesus helps explain how Goan Catholicism should not be seen as merely a product of European conversion.

As Savia Viegas has eruditely and painstakingly catalogued, da Fonseca was keen on showing how the artist’s “ordinary” looking biblical figures, brown-skinned and garbed in the clothing of working-class South Asians, were evidence of the localisation of Christianity over several centuries. The art da Fonseca produced is far from ordinary, of course. Its beauty is in the relaying of the simplicities of everyday devotion. Concomitantly, the Blue Jesus event in Midnight’s Children stages a quotidian exchange within the local church, one that is about God’s existence during troubling political times. Intermedially, Rushdie and da Fonseca deepen our understanding of the long history of Catholicism in South Asia.

In Chapter 4, you take a different intermedial turn, reading Yazoo’s “ Only You ” (1982) and its a cappella cover by The Flying Pickets alongside Marcella D’Souza’s experience of Thatcherite England in A Girl from Zanzibar . You trace the song through its two lives: as a synthpop romance of aspiration and as a miners’ strike anthem. In the same chapter, you connect Marcella’s 1983 arrival in England to Margaret Thatcher’s simultaneous visit to Goa for CHOGM , held at Fort Aguada Beach Resort, which you describe as “built in the 1970s within the ruins of a Portuguese-era fort.” How do you see the relationship between the sonic and the spatial in that chapter, and what made you reach for a pop song as a critical tool alongside the art history? The most direct answer to your question is that I could not get that Yazoo earworm out of my head! Really, there were just too many delicious coincidences: the years in which the song was released and the events of the novel unfold, and then the similarity between the lyrics and the description of an incident that transpires very early on in the book. There was just no getting away from hearing the song in the book, again explaining how intermediality works in our engagement of even the literary.

Then, as I delved deeper into the song and learned about The Flying Pickets, their social justice connections, and the strange connection between their acapella version of “Only You” and Thatcher herself, it was a fait accompli – the song became an organi s ing rubric in that chapter, which is one I am quite fond of.

The sonic history of “Only You” reverberates through the various geographic points referenced in the chapter – Goa, England, Zanzibar – as a metaphor for a postcolonial new world order. Its rhythm entwines with the braided spatial histories that King’s novel relies on (some unwittingly) – the Fort Aguada, an abandoned Napoleonic-era British cemetery in Dona Paula, and then the labour history of the miners’ strikes of the 1970s and 1980s in England – to ask questions of globalisation. A major one is: how much better has globalisation made the lives of working-class people? The answer is damning. In being about neoliberal globalisation, this chapter also underscores how Goan postnationalism is not only about Goa and Goans.

Your position at William & Mary spans English, Asian and Pacific Islander American Studies, and affiliated roles in Global Studies and Gender, Sexuality, and Women’s Studies. You have described this interdisciplinarity as something you hope the book itself mirrors, writing that you want to “link disparate geopolitical areas of study.” In the book, this plays out practically: the introduction draws on Indian Ocean studies, the Rushdie chapter on art history, the Vassanji chapter on educational and labour history in East Africa, and the King chapter on Thatcherite housing policy. How does the experience of teaching across these fields shape the scholarship, and does the book in turn change how you teach? Another very good question. The classroom is a space of exchange. Even when I may not incorporate the specific novels I research into my syllabi, I am still thinking about the questions that animate my scholarship. This comes out in my interactions with students in the various fields in which I instruct; the boundaries between the disciplines are present but fluid. For research to work, it must translate into dialogue – the classroom is a venue for nurturing discourse.

It is unfortunate that the study of Goan literature or Goan representation in cultural production is so limited. One is hard-pressed to locate courses of this nature that are offered consistently in Goa or anywhere else. In lieu of this, what I hope my book offers is a method for me and others to continue developing how we understand Goan subjectivity in its evocations of multiplicity. Ultimately, the purpose of Across Continents is to harness Goan subjectivity as an analytic through which to understand difference through interdisciplinarity.

The book acknowledges that its focus is exclusively anglophone, and your endnotes note that Goan writing in Konkani, Marathi, and Portuguese warrants further scholarly attention. Three of the four novelists you study are not themselves Goan. The concluding chapter on Skin opens a confrontation with Goan bourgeois complicity in the Portuguese slave trade that feels like the beginning of a larger conversation rather than the end of one. And the acknowledgements close with a visit to occupied Palestine that you describe as having “changed everything I thought I knew about coloniality despite having been a scholar of it for years.” As conversations about displacement, citizenship, and colonial afterlives intensify globally, how do you see the book speaking to the contemporary moment? And where does this go next? Is there a second book forming? There is always more work to be done on all these subjects! It is remarkable that for such a small region, there are so many languages to consider, such a wide diaspora, and an incredible entanglement with global history. Increasingly, scholarship on Goa has been building bridges across these multiple terrains – my book would not have been possible had I not relied on the hard work of many talented academics and researchers across several fields. But yes, when it comes to thinking about the multilingual ecosystem that undergirds Goan multiplicity, this is an area that is as daunting as it is promising.

As I have said already, I hope that those who look to Across Continents to learn about Goan subjectivity also learn much more than this for, as I have been highlighting, subjectivity for only its own sake is simply identity politics. In connecting coloniality in Palestine to Goan diasporic history, this is not something that is just an academic exercise or one that taps into a cause du jour; instead, it is integral to my book’s conception of understanding oppression and its undoing. I am also not the first to make these connections; my book mentions Violet Dias Lannoy (1925-1972), who, during her lifetime, was shunned for seeing a common cause between the freedom of Palestinians and Goan anticolonialism.

I have slowly begun formulating a new set of ideas as I move forward and, unsurprisingly, I have been thinking about more research in art history. I look forward to developing that canvas further.

Oriana Fernandez is a chartered architect and urban designer based in London. She trained at the Goa College of Architecture and holds an MArch (Urban Design) from CEPT University, Gujarat, and an MA Urban Design from the University of Westminster, London. She writes on architectural design and education, governance and professional culture for Building Design and maintains a Substack.

editorials.title: ‘Shake off the aura’: Novelist Amitabha Bagchi on originality and borrowing in literary writing
editorials.passage:
As per Umberto Eco, “Books always speak of other books, and every story tells a story that has already been told.” Eco neglected to mention if books only speak of other books, and if it is okay if they do, or should the authors of books that largely speak of other books be hauled over the coals, indicted for their crime and given punishments that are less stringent than those handed out to common plagiarists, but are punishments nonetheless. Had he done so, we wouldn’t have to face the conundrum raised by Urdu novelist Asha’ar Najmi’s long piece (in Hindi) on Khalid Javed’s oeuvre whose thrust is that several of Javed’s wonderfully original-seeming ideas across five novels can be traced back to novelists, thinkers, graphic novelists and filmmakers from the West. The conundrum, stated plainly, is this: What constitutes originality in fiction? More specifically: If an author directly borrows ideas or settings from another author, wrapping them in his own setting and his own style, is that a form of fraud?

If we transpose the question to academic writing, the answer is a clear yes. If there is an idea that is published in the literature and you present it as your own, that’s not allowed. It’s the journal reviewer’s job to prevent it from happening, and if the reviewer fails, the journal is still duty-bound to issue an erratum or withdraw the paper if such a claim is made. On the literary side, things run in the opposite direction. I have never heard anyone say “That Tulsidas’s Ramcharitmanas is just a total ripoff of Valmiki!” or “Did you know Girish Karnad pulled the whole story of Agni aur Barkha out of the Mahabharata and just redid it as a play? What a scam!” And so I was somewhat perplexed as Najmi took us through all the references in great detail. And what a list of references it is! Thomas Bernhard to Emile Zola to Neil Gaiman, Kafka and Bachelard among others. Peter Greenaway and Roman Polanski do the honours from the filmmaking side of things. My own taste in literary criticism runs to the genealogy of writings and so I really enjoyed reading the essay and trying to follow the connections it made. At the end of it, I am not convinced that Najmi’s demonstration of these connections destroys Javed’s reputation as a novelist.

Just the other day on Instagram, I came across a video where a guitar player was showing how the melody of the 1956 classic song from CID “ Ye hai Bombay meri jaan ” – whose lines “zara hatke/zara bach ke ” continue to define that city despite its change of name – is a straight lift of the American folk song “ Clementine .” I have to admit I felt a kind of shame that a cultural artefact that I value so much turns out to greatly lack originality. And here the lift is of the melody, which is plagiarism to the best of my knowledge.

Hindi films used to do this regularly, back before the Internet turned the whole world into a village, and we have all shared in this feeling of second-classness when yet another Indian film song is revealed to have been a copy of a Western one (my personal favourite: compare the opening riff of the song “ Kaisi hai ye rut ” from Dil Chahta Hai to the riff from the song “ Forty or fifty horses ” by the Spin Doctors). My postcolonial – but not fully decolonised – mind tells me that if the copying was from Indian sources, or even Persian, Arabic or Turkic sources, or, like the great Bengali artists Abanindranath Tagore and others, from East Asian sources, the shame would have come in an attenuated form. It may even have been reversed: When Yesudas sings “Ka karoon sajni,” we know he is singing a version of a thumri sung earlier by Bade Ghulam Ali Khan, and this makes us proud rather than ashamed: we accept it as a fitting act of homage. But when Bappi Lahiri copies “ Video Killed the Radio Star ” in “ Koi yahaan naache naache ”, our heads hang in shame. That’s who we still are. So, I do understand Najmi’s great disappointment that an author whose work’s originality he so greatly admired turned out to have borrowed thoughts extensively from various Western sources. That’s where the anger may be coming from, the anger inherent in the claim that the “innocent” Urdu reading public – a group Najmi too belonged to before extensive reading made him lose his innocence – has been defrauded.

My submission would be that perhaps Najmi is, in his understandable disappointment, setting the bar so high that no author would be able to jump over it. Even the authors of the Mahabharata or the Epic of Gilgamesh or Homer, who wrote the currently-back-in-fashion Odyssey (ripped off by those damned Coen brothers for their movie O Brother Where Art Thou ), probably had oral or other texts they were pulling from, mercifully lost now; otherwise, they too would run the risk of being cancelled. My suggestion would be to shake off that aura, that sense born of ignorance that these works were extremely original, and re-read them for what they are, intertexts with books the author has read, and evaluate them the way all literature should be evaluated: by asking the question of whether it is true to its time and place.

If you’re still reading, you may be wondering why a public attack by one Urdu novelist on another published in a Hindi journal is of any interest to an English novelist. The prosaic reason is that 20% of a question raised in this piece is directed at me. The question is in the context of Javed’s novel Nematkhana, translated into English as Paradise of Food, which won the JCB Prize in 2022. The prize’s five-member jury included me that year. After showing how closely related the work is to the work of the French writer Michel Tournier (quite closely) and to the novel The Cook by Henry Kressing (not so closely), Najmi asks: Was there not one person in the JCB Prize jury who had read Michel Tournier or Henry Kressing? I can’t answer for the other four, but I can say that I certainly haven’t read either; in fact, I hadn’t even heard their names. Knowing how the connections between books give me great pleasure, my sense is that if I had read Tournier or Kressing’s books it might have made me like Paradise of Food better, but that’s pure speculation. One way of getting a more definitive answer to this question might come from the jury of the DSC Prize, who gave my novel Half the Night Is Gone the prize in 2019. I could ask them whether they had read Amritlal Nagar’s Amrit aur Vish and whether they had noted that I had directly picked up the device of a novelist who is grieving his son from it. Or maybe I shouldn’t. Just like Najmi says of Javed’s various literary sources, I have long since “digested” that money.

But, seriously speaking, what struck me about Najmi’s essay is that he presents himself as someone who had placed Javed on a very high pedestal because he didn’t realise that many of Javed’s ideas came from the books he had read and the movies he had seen. And because he had built up an impossible image of the writer, his disappointment overflows and his well-researched and enlightening piece is shot through with a bitterness which undermines its erudition. “Bhakti in religion may be a path to salvation,” Ambedkar had said. “But in politics bhakti, or hero-worship, is a sure road to degradation.” Similarly, I feel writers and writing should not be treated with too much reverence, not by readers and not by other writers. Dilawar Figar, who loves Ghalib, says

jo chāhte haiñ ki fauq-ul-bashar banā deñ use hameñ to us ke un ahbāb se bhī shikva hai

(those who want to make a superman of him/I take issue with those friends of him)

Eventually, as writers, we need to read each other with generosity and compassion, with neither hero-worship nor disdain, and with the hope that what we read will nourish us and lead us to still other books that we didn’t know of, or didn’t realise would resonate with us. And now, if you will excuse me, I need to go and find a copy of that Bachelard book that I hadn’t heard of before I read Najmi’s essay.

This article first appeared on the author’s Substack .

editorials.title: ‘The River of Grey Flowers’: Good intentions do not always a good novel make
editorials.passage:
Reading The River of Grey Flowers feels a lot like watching Dhurandhar . While Rejimon Kuttappan’s debut novel has none of Aditya Dhar’s right-wing nationalism, it succumbs to the same fatal flaw in narrative: it depends so much on its events being true stories that it fails to create enough stakes for the characters within its fiction.

Kuttappan is an investigative journalist specialising in migrant rights and forced labour, and this novel borrows from much of the news he has broken. It follows John Easow, a Dalit fisherman’s son, who is a graphic designer by day and turmeric smuggler by night. When he falls in love with Thenmozhi, a savarna woman from the neighbouring village, they marry in secret; he is forced to give up his boat, and therefore his income from smuggling, in exchange for his life. He loses his day job too, and applies to another graphic design role in Dubai – this takes him to Thailand, and then, against his will, to Myawaddy, or Myanmar.

His new role is a forced labour scheme, where he is made to defraud strangers online alongside similarly deceived Dalit and African workers. He poses as different women using different SIM cards, and sweet-talks men into sending him money. There are daily targets and monthly targets; if these are not met, or if the workers are found trying to escape, they are brutally beaten, tortured, and even killed.

This is a space with no regard for human dignity, and the story’s emotional crux lies in the intimacies and solidarities that people forge within it – for instance, when John and an African colleague, Guta, discuss the music they love, which also happens to accompany their respective resistance movements back home. It is also guided by the urge to return, that potent tug towards families and lovers left behind, exacerbated for John as he discovers that Thenmozhi is pregnant with their child.

However, the weight of these conditions is felt by inference – you experience pain insofar as you know these are painful things to experience. (Like in Dhurandhar : you go “ouch” when Ranveer Singh is being beaten up, but still have no personal backstory, no reason to root for his victory other than his Indian citizenship.) Kuttappan’s efforts to bridge the gap between you and John are either absent or grossly unsuccessful, neglecting what could’ve been a powerful exploration of John’s inner life and choosing instead to haphazardly narrate the events around him. The tone is stilted, the metaphors out of place, and this prevents you from being fully immersed in his world.

I was particularly disappointed by the sequence that leads John to Myanmar, because it fails to answer the question it is supposed to. What compels him to go overseas without his wife, when he can find jobs closer to home? If his intercaste marriage has made him a pariah in his village, surely there must be somewhere else he can go; and if he is expressly looking for the financial gain that the Gulf promises, surely there can be a mention of it? The Dubai role is casually suggested to him by a friend, who shows him that the job description goes beyond Facebook posts, asking for logos, layouts, and colour palettes. “Order where my life had been only motion”, John thinks, and then thinks of Thenmozhi’s words (which words exactly? We aren’t clear). He applies. Is that all the consideration it takes to make such a life-altering call?

It seems so, because the novel goes on to restate its premise as though the reader has already forgotten it: “What began as a Dubai interview carried me through Bangkok and ended in something no contract had named – slavery, stripped of glamour and disguised as opportunity.” John is narrating his story in retrospect, and with a nonlinear timeline, so I suppose such reflection is warranted on occasion; but it interrupts the meat of the story too often to land successfully. In fact, the novel is full of asides like this, which fail at creating emotional depth, furthering narrative, or establishing the way John sees the world (what, in writers’ workshop terms, would be called characterisation and voice). So really, the novel is full of chaff.

I must say at this point that Kuttappan is a brilliant journalist who reports with great empathy. We have him to thank for thousands of migrant labourers’ lives coming to light, and this extensive coverage is detailed in his other book, Undocumented: Stories of Indian Migrants in the Arab Gulf. Take, for instance, the story of Appuni , a migrant worker in Oman who longed to return to his family in Kerala. His passport had been handed over to his sponsor, and when he did return under an amnesty scheme 22 years later, he was shunned because he had not made enough money. In just a few quotes, his shame and loneliness are clear, and they moved me deeply; this excerpt let me inhabit a richer emotional landscape than all of the novel.

When such stories are told as reportage, they are a method to express a larger truth: that our country’s most vulnerable groups are sold promises of dignity and financial stability, only to be subjected to exploitative working conditions. In fiction, the opposite movement must take place, distilling a larger truth to a singular life. The borders between the two styles are porous (they are ultimately both stories), but the charge of fiction is to yoke its reader to its characters. I wanted, in these 250-odd pages, to care about John, ask what he will do next, what might happen to him. But I ended up caring about forced labour – in itself a noble and necessary concern, just not enough to warrant being a novel.

The River … has its poignant moments, but they are needles in its haystack of digression and awkward prose. Perhaps a kinder reader will locate them with more ease than I did, and will find in John the echoes of Appuni, and thousands like him.

The River of Grey Flowers, Rejimon Kuttappan, Speaking Tiger Books.

editorials.title: Who is AI being built for? Why employees hesitate to adopt it
editorials.passage:
What if the problem with AI adoption begins before anyone is asked to adopt it?

Organisations are spending heavily on AI and deploying it across their operations, yet many employees still struggle to make these tools useful in everyday work. The usual diagnosis is poor adoption, leading to calls for more training, better incentives and stronger change management.

A recent large-scale study by Cohere Labs points to a deeper, long-standing problem in technology development: technical feasibility remains a powerful filter for deciding what gets built. The study found that barely 2.6 per cent of AI tools can fully automate specified occupational tasks end-to-end.

Tools are often designed around what machines can do before anyone asks what workers need them to do. This builder-first logic has shaped technology development for decades. That logic becomes increasingly problematic as AI moves from assisting individual tasks to performing parts of the work itself.

Boston Consulting Group’s research sheds light on the other side of the equation. Once AI enters an organisation, its value depends heavily on how people use it, how work is organised and how responsibilities change. The missing piece is how human behaviour and workflow design shape AI adoption.

Taken together with Cohere’s findings, a difficult inference emerges: employees may be expected to adapt to tools that were never designed around the realities of their work. This may explain part of the persistent gap between AI adoption, usage and business value.
What gets built first?
In a large-scale study released in September 2026, Cohere Labs examined 696,291 tools across 123,069 publicly listed Model Context Protocol, or MCP, servers. Under a strict definition of automation, only 2.6 per cent could perform a recognised occupational task from beginning to end. Of 923 US occupations studied, 419 had no agentic-tool activity in the public dataset.
For 65 occupations where Cohere compared worker preferences with expert assessments of AI capability, tool supply tracked technical feasibility more closely than workers’ preferences about which tasks they wanted automated. This doesn’t mean developers ignore workers. It suggests that, within the occupations studied, what AI can accomplish has influenced tool supply more strongly than what workers want automated.
The study has limits. It covers publicly listed MCP tools rather than proprietary systems, but offers a large-scale view of how technical possibilities become workplace capabilities.
AI supply is not workplace demand
A tool catalogue tells an organisation what exists. It does not tell it whether a capability belongs in a particular workflow. An AI system may draft a legal document, analyse complaints or generate code. The technical question is whether the output is good enough. The workplace questions are different: Who checks it? What happens when it is uncertain? Who remains accountable? What happens to the junior employee who previously learned the profession by doing the task?
Removing such activities can improve efficiency while weakening another part of the work system. Repetitive tasks can expose inexperienced employees to larger processes. Manual review can control errors.
Cohere also found that agentic tools differ across occupations. In healthcare and computing, they tend to reach more specialised tasks; in legal, production and sales, they remain closer to routine work. That could affect how workers gain or lose expertise. The question is what a task contributes to the wider job, not merely whether it can be automated.
Put behaviour into the build
Behavioural analysis should enter AI development before deployment. Developers need to study how people work, make decisions and respond to uncertainty. Asking employees whether they like a system is insufficient.
Before building workplace AI, organisations should identify which activities employees want automated, assisted or retained. They should observe where professional judgement enters the workflow and where actual work differs from the formal process. Learning deserves particular attention. If AI removes routine tasks, it may also remove experiences through which people acquire expertise. A system that makes experienced employees faster could make it harder for inexperienced employees to become experienced.
Start with the work
Organisations buying AI face a similar trap. Vendor demonstrations make it easy to begin with the product and search for a use case afterwards. The better starting point is the work.

Organisations need to know what current AI systems can perform, where they can assist and where human coordination remains essential. That assessment should be made against real workflows rather than generic claims. The relevant questions are direct: What can AI do, where could it fit, and what would change? Employees who perform the work should help answer the questions.
What happens after deployment?
BCG’s 2025 Build for the Future x AI study found that only about 5 per cent of organisations reported substantial financial gains from AI. Its 10-20-70 success framework assigns roughly 10 per cent of transformation effort to algorithms, 20 per cent to technology and 70 per cent to changes involving people.

BCG’s May 2026 research found a striking perception gap: 76 per cent of executives believed employees were excited about AI, while only 31% of employees said they were. The gap points to a problem that extends beyond technical capability. AI enters existing systems of trust, authority and responsibility, and how people interpret it can influence how they use it, check its outputs and assign responsibility for its failures. Human behaviour therefore plays a central role in whether AI adoption produces sustained business value.
From deployment to feedback
AI development needs a stronger connection between building and observing. Builders should examine how people use systems, where they override them and where they create workarounds. Organisations should feed that evidence into workflow design and technology choices.

Workers should not decide what gets built. User preference is one input; technical feasibility, economics, safety, regulation and strategy still matter. Behavioural evidence should enter design early and remain part of it after deployment.
Cohere provides the upstream warning: in the occupations it examined, the public agentic ecosystem reflected technical feasibility more strongly than worker preference. BCG provides the downstream evidence: organisations capture AI value through changes in people, processes and behaviour.
The critical behavioural and workflow tests
Workplace AI therefore needs two tests, one before the tool is built and another before it is scaled.

The first should examine the work itself: What does the workflow require? Which tasks should AI automate, assist or leave unchanged? Where does human judgement matter? What skills could disappear if a task is removed? Which responsibilities would need to be reassigned?

The second should examine what happens after deployment. How are employees using the system? Where are they over-trusting it, resisting it or creating workarounds? Has accountability shifted? Does the redesigned workflow actually improve the outcome the AI investment was intended to deliver? If the technology changes how a task is performed, the workflow around that task may also need to change.

Together, these tests create a feedback loop between technology, behaviour and work: build, observe, redesign and build again. The objective is not simply to measure whether employees use AI, but to determine whether the technology and the workflow have evolved together.

The important question for AI development therefore extends beyond ‘Can we automate this?’ It should ask: ‘What will happen to the work when we do, and how should the workflow change with it?’

Human behaviour and workflow design should become integral to AI design, rather than being treated as implementation concerns. Organisations need to decide what AI should automate, what they should buy and which work should remain human.
The institutional principle is straightforward: design AI around the work it enters, and treat workers’ behaviour as evidence from the beginning. That may finally close the stubborn gap between AI adoption and the business value organisations expect from it.

(Sreejith Sreedharan is a technology analyst and author of ‘Future of Work – AI Augmented Autonomous Decentralised’. He works on organisational AI readiness and created the AI Instinct Index®, a psychometric diagnostic designed to assess behavioural readiness for AI adoption and adaptive capacity in constraint-heavy environments. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Trump is disrupting the old world order, Brics must build the new
editorials.passage:
“Geopolitical vacuums come with an expiry date. Brics cannot afford to spend this one drafting another communiqué.”

Nature, Aristotle is said to have observed, abhors a vacuum. Geopolitics does too. When established powers retreat, institutions weaken and old rules begin to lose their legitimacy, the space they leave behind does not remain unoccupied for long.
That is what makes the Brics Summit in New Delhi this weekend unusually consequential. The grouping meets not simply amid another period of geopolitical turbulence, but at a moment when some of the assumptions underpinning the post-Cold War international order are being openly contested.

With Donald Trump in the White House, tariffs have returned as instruments of geopolitical coercion, economic interdependence is increasingly weaponised, wars have exposed the impotence of international institutions, and the competition between Washington and Beijing is forcing countries to reconsider everything from supply chains to strategic alignments. American isolationism and its transactional approach have exposed the Western bloc to multi-pronged leakages and unprecedented disunity.

At the outset, Brics is not an anti-West arrangement. However, for two decades, Brics has argued that the world needs to become more plural. Today, unusually, the world is giving it an opportunity to make that argument material. The question is whether Brics knows what to do with it. Because geopolitical vacuums come with an expiry date. International orders eventually settle. Countries adjust to new realities and what once appeared negotiable becomes institutionalised again. The window through which the international system can be meaningfully reshaped is therefore considerably smaller than the rhetoric of summits sometimes suggests. Therefore, Brics cannot afford to spend this one drafting another communiqué.
Exploit The Trump Factor
Trump is relevant here not simply because he is “anti-multilateral”. He is a disruptor of the very order Brics has complained about for two decades. The United States finds itself consumed by a crisis in West Asia, while the war in Eastern Europe continues to absorb European political attention, military resources and fiscal capacity. Beyond both theatres sits the much larger structural challenge of China and the Indo-Pacific. Washington is therefore being forced to reconcile global commitments accumulated under an earlier distribution of power with a world in which its resources and attention are increasingly contested.

This is where the Trump factor becomes particularly consequential. Trump’s answer to overstretch is not necessarily withdrawal. It is reprioritisation: make allies pay more, treat trade as leverage, rebuild industrial capacity, secure critical supply chains and reconsider commitments that no longer deliver sufficient strategic returns. In other words, Washington is attempting to make American primacy cheaper, harder and more transactional.

That process creates friction, and friction creates openings. For Brics, this may be one of them. For much of its existence, Brics could afford incrementalism. It could issue declarations demanding greater representation for the Global South, call periodically for reform of the Bretton Woods institutions and gradually experiment with alternatives such as the New Development Bank. Western primacy appeared sufficiently entrenched that there was little realistic prospect of overturning it anyway. That luxury may no longer exist.

Brics therefore faces a race against institutional inertia. The more important question is whether, while the distribution of global power remains unusually fluid, Brics can construct enough financial, technological, commercial and diplomatic alternatives that the next international order cannot simply be written without it.
Brics Needs More Than Common Ground
Before Brics begins imagining itself as the architect of an alternative world order, it must confront an uncomfortable question: do its own members trust one another enough to build one?

For all the language of solidarity that accompanies Brics summits, the grouping remains constrained by enormous internal contradictions. India and China speak of multipolarity while carrying the memory of deadly confrontations along their disputed border and continuing to regard each other as strategic competitors. Iran and the Gulf states may share a Brics table, but West Asia tensions and competing interests when it comes to the US do not disappear with membership.

These are not cosmetic differences. They go to the heart of whether Brics can ever become more than the sum of its grievances. A grouping does not become a geopolitical pole because its leaders stand together for a photograph. Nor does a larger membership necessarily mean greater power. There is little strategic value in displaying unity while preparing contingencies against one another back home.
If Brics genuinely wants to build an alternative architecture, therefore, its first infrastructure project must be trust. That does not require its members to become allies. Brics was never meant to become Nato, and attempting to manufacture that kind of ideological or military cohesion would probably destroy the grouping. It does, however, require that economic dependencies will not readily become instruments of coercion; that borders will not periodically become theatres of limited war; and that participation in common institutions will survive bilateral crises.

India-China relations are the most important test. Beijing cannot simultaneously speak the language of Global South solidarity and expect New Delhi to compartmentalise Chinese aggression along the Line of Actual Control. India, similarly, cannot be expected to invest its strategic future in institutions whose reliability ultimately depends upon a country it must simultaneously prepare to deter.

No amount of rhetoric about multipolarity can overcome that contradiction. You cannot build an alternative financial architecture upon a strategic architecture of mutual suspicion. Before dreaming of a common currency, create dependable payment windows between members. Before promising a new world order, create alternative channels through which trade can continue during periods of global financial disruption. Make payment systems interoperable. Build mechanisms for emergency liquidity and trade finance. Develop resilient supply chains in energy, food, pharmaceuticals and critical minerals.

In other words, build capability before symbolism. Imagine the contradiction otherwise: a grouping seeks to persuade the developing world that it can provide a stable alternative to Western-led institutions while two of its largest members contemplate military contingencies against each other. Capital notices political risk. Governments notice strategic risk. Businesses notice whether payment corridors and supply chains can survive the next border crisis.

An alternative order has to be dependable before it can be alternative.
Brics Needs Institutional Muscle
The West’s great structural advantage has never simply been that Western countries agree on everything. They do not. It is that decades of institution-building created mechanisms through which disagreement could occur without destroying the architecture underneath it. Financial systems, climate commitments, capital markets, security arrangements, commercial networks and institutions accumulated credibility because governments and businesses expected them to continue functioning tomorrow.

Brics needs to acquire that same institutional muscle memory. One payment corridor at a time. One development loan at a time. One supply-chain agreement at a time. Brics already has the population, resources, markets and geopolitical weight.
What it has this weekend is something considerably rarer: a moment when the distribution of global power is genuinely unsettled. There is a reason to approach that moment with confidence. Brics has travelled an improbable distance from an investment-bank acronym to a forum that some of the world’s most consequential states consider worth investing political capital in. The last two decades were about giving the Global South a larger voice. The next must be about giving that voice institutional weight.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Don’t buy the optics: To view Xi’s visit as a ‘reset’ would be a dangerous miscalculation
editorials.passage:
China’s strategic culture differs from the West, and certainly from that of the United States. So, where a Donald Trump would telegraph intent and scream in capital letters on Truth Social, or a Scott Bessent would write an opinion piece in the Financial Times explaining American policy on Iran, Beijing would make subtle, almost imperceptible moves that are nevertheless pregnant with significance.
I am thinking about Indian ambassador to China Vikram Doraswami’s recent column in Global Times, the Chinese state-owned newspaper. Forget about the content of the column, which in itself is noteworthy; the fact that the Chinese Communist Party allowed its media outlet to carry the point of view of an Indian envoy should tell you that China is giving signals.

Those signals became almost too loud to ignore as Xi Jinping touched down in India on Saturday after a gap of seven years. A bevy of Chinese journalists, some of whom had arrived earlier, were talking about how “clean New Delhi is” and giving enthusiastic bites on India-China friendship. “We are friends, not rivals,” said a beaming Li Jingjing, stressing that the “world is looking at China-India cooperation.” Wenting Xie, another journalist, said, “the visit is a very important opportunity to further improve bilateral ties.”

Mao Ning, China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, upon landing in New Delhi, was posting touristy pictures on X, while reports emerged, coincidentally, I’m sure, that China Southern Airlines will resume Guangzhou-Delhi flights after six years. This is no longer signalling, but full-steam wooing of India by the Chinese Communist Party with a degree of coordination that is impossible in democracies.

Which ideally should make one a little uncomfortable. Why is China suddenly projecting an image of friendship and warmth? Count me a cynic, but I’d rather wallow in cynicism than be vulnerable to one more backstabbing. Unfortunately, our public discourse never fails to miss the wood for the trees. As Xi’s aeroplane landed on the tarmac for the 18th Brics Summit, media buzz swirled around the possibility of a diplomatic “reset”.

After years of frozen ties, military standoffs in the high Himalayas and simmering geopolitical hostility, the optics of the Chinese president and the Indian prime minister sharing a stage on Indian soil for the first time in seven years naturally invite optimism.

Pundits and eager observers are quick to interpret every handshake, every bilateral sideline meeting, and every joint communiqué as the dawn of a renewed partnership. But viewing this summit through the lens of a fundamental reset is not just premature; it is a dangerous miscalculation.

The cold, structural realities of the world’s most complex and consequential bilateral relationship have not gone away. What we are watching unfold before our eyes is not a return to the heady optimism of Mamallapuram. It is, rather, a calibrated, cautious re-engagement.

For India, the immediate objective is to stabilise a volatile diplomatic relationship and bring a semblance of balance to an increasingly lopsided bilateral trade architecture.

China has surpassed the United States to become India’s largest trading partner, with total bilateral trade hitting a historic record of $151.1 billion in the fiscal year ending March 2026. Simultaneously, India’s trade deficit with China has surged to an all-time high of $112.16 billion, climbing from $99.21 billion the previous year.
New Delhi operates with absolutely no illusions about China’s long-term geopolitical posture. The aim right now is simply to manage the temperature, prevent accidental kinetic escalation along the disputed frontier and safeguard domestic economic interests from structural vulnerabilities.

Beijing, on the other hand, views this diplomatic schmooze as a tactical re-engagement, and it is showing earnestness for a reason. For the CCP, this is a necessary, if temporary, manoeuvre to clear the path for unrestricted access to the Indian market.

Facing an escalating trade war with the US, a sluggish domestic economy and the global reorganisation of supply chains, Beijing needs new avenues for its industrial overcapacity. As the largest economy in South Asia and the world’s fastest-growing consumer market, India represents a critical economic pressure valve.

Beijing is also aware that the sustenance of BRICS as a functional, non-Western multilateral platform is crucial to its broader geopolitical agenda. Consider the carefully synchronised statements being made by the Chinese journalists in India. According to Wenting of Global Times, “China fully supports India’s work as Chair and is ready to work with all parties to promote this great BRICS cooperation. As you have mentioned, India is the Chair this year, and China fully supports India’s presidency.”

China has invested heavily in positioning Brics as the vanguard of an alternative multipolar world order that challenges Western financial and institutional hegemony. Without India’s active and heavyweight participation, Brics risks becoming a hollow, China-centric echo chamber rather than the formidable geopolitical bloc Beijing envisions. Xi’s overtures of friendship and warmth in New Delhi are therefore designed specifically to achieve those objectives.

On the economic front, “unrestricted access” remains a one-way street. While China pushes aggressively for frictionless entry into India’s markets, Beijing has simultaneously strengthened an impenetrable web of non-tariff barriers to shut out Indian pharmaceuticals, IT services, and agricultural exports.

This deliberate asymmetry has reinforced a massive, structural trade deficit. Beijing weaponises its monopoly over critical minerals, restricts the export of heavy infrastructure equipment, and arbitrarily delays or denies visas for Indian engineers working on crucial joint ventures.

This weaponisation of trade adds another layer of mistrust, proving that commercial interdependence with China remains a strategic vulnerability. These competing signals — of warm sound bites, smiles and bonhomie in New Delhi against the backdrop of militarised borders, military support to Pakistan, maritime encirclement, and economic coercion — put into sharp relief the structural realities of bilateral ties.

To the extent possible, Brics provides a necessary opportunity to iron out the most severe creases in the bilateral relationship. It allows both sides to lower the temperature, resume direct lines of communication, and project an image of global statesmanship to the Global South.

I would firmly categorise this bilateral meeting as temporary conflict management, not conflict resolution. The fundamentals of the India-China relationship remain overwhelmingly adversarial.

Beyond the media buzz of a ‘historic turning point’, New Delhi knows that what lies ahead is not a renewed era of ‘brotherly cooperation’, but a tense, protracted phase of competitive coexistence, regardless of the smiling optics on display or a handshake on the sidelines of the summit.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: 25 Years After 9/11, the War on Terror Has Left a More Dangerous World
editorials.passage: The 25th anniversary of 11 September 2001—the enormity that saw the Twin Towers in New York collapsing after an audacious jihadi terrorist attack—is an opportune moment to reflect on the many anomalies, extraordinary incongruities, and tragic ironies that have punctuated the 9/11 trajectory.On that ill-fated day, 25 years ago, the world stood united. The attack on the US was seen as a brutal assault on the very idea of a modern, open society. The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) Resolution 1368, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) invoking Article 5 for the first and only time, and the global outpouring of support: Washington enjoyed empathy and credibility in spades.The Global War on Terror (GWOT) was not seen as a US-led war but as one against a medieval ideology that used jihadi terror as an instrument. The perpetrators, Al-Qaeda and its chief Osama bin Laden, and the Taliban regime in Kabul that provided sanctuary, were zealously prosecuted by the US-led coalition.November, Terrorism, and Pakistan: Why The Ghosts of 26/11 Still Haunt Us Osama bin Laden is central to the 9/11 trajectory. In 2001-2002, he was made into the devil incarnate—the most wanted man on earth, the face of global jihad, the reason GWOT was launched. And then, incongruously, he fades out of the US narrative. The Bush team gets distracted by Iraq, resources shift, and the bin Laden's hunt goes cold. The supreme irony, the anomaly that sums up GWOT, is that after a decade of war in Afghanistan, bin Laden is finally found not in a cave in Tora Bora, but in a comfortable safe-house in Abbottabad, next to Pakistan's premier military academy. The ISI maintained it had no inkling whatsoever, but the world knew better about the architect of that double game: the Pakistani Army Chief General Pervez Musharra.Musharraf fine-tuned the ability to hunt with the hounds and run with the hare to an art form. Within months of 9/11, he convinced Washington he was their indispensable ally, so much so that Pakistan was designated a Major Non-NATO Ally (MNNA) in 2004. Musharraf, the skilled salesman, also convinced the Pentagon that the Pakistan Army was on their side in the GWOT, while simultaneously signalling to the Taliban and to jihadi groups that their cause was being protected and their leadership given sanctuary in Quetta and Karachi.The tragic irony was that the US was inadvertently funding the Pakistan Army, which provided tactical support to the adversary, resulting in many US casualties.That duplicitous diplomacy is the original incongruity of GWOT. While the US bombed Afghanistan with impunity, its critical supply lines, intelligence cooperation, and political cover depended on Rawalpindi (global headquarters of the Pakistan Army), which was nurturing the very enemy.For Delhi, the 11 September 2001 bookmark is critical. Barely three months after 9/11, on 13 December, the Indian Parliament was attacked by jihadi terror groups nurtured by the same establishment that was cosying up to the US. While the world rallied around the US in its GWOT, India was waging a more lonely campaign against terrorism.In December 1999, the Vajpayee government swallowed the ignominy of a hostage exchange, after the hijack of Air India flight IC 814. Delhi was compelled to release Pakistan-trained jihadi terrorists to a safe haven in Afghanistan then under the Taliban rule. It was evident that India had few meaningful options to contain the terror challenge, and the GWOT was a welcome development for a weary Delhi.However, the central, unlearned lesson of the past three decades is what this author had termed at the time as NWET, which stands for Nuclear Weapon Enabled Terrorism.Pakistan discovered that nuclear weapons are not just a deterrent against full-scale war, but a shield behind which jihadi terrorism can be waged with impunity. Every major attack—Parliament 2001, Mumbai 2008, Pulwama 2019, and Pahalgam April 2025—follows the same template: inflict mass casualties through proxies, then immediately invoke the threat of nuclear escalation to forestall Indian retaliation and invite the international community to counsel restraint.GWOT floundered because it never confronted NWET. It punished a non-nuclear Afghanistan for harbouring bin Laden, chased a mirage in Iraq at enormous cost but rewarded a nuclear Pakistan that institutionalised terrorism as state policy. The war bombed Kabul to the 'stone age' but gave Islamabad billions in aid and MNNA status for helping hunt bin Laden that Rawalpindi was hiding.An uncomfortable question that arises is: did the US fall for this post 9/11 Pakistani perfidy due to professional ineptitude or institutional turpitude?US-Ind-Pak: Obama Unveiled Pak Treachery Over Bin Laden & Nukes, Embraced IndiaIronically, the cost of those lapses was strategic. While the US bled over $2.3 trillion in Afghanistan-Pakistan and lost precious lives, China grew from $1.3 trillion GDP to over $17 trillion in the period 2001-2021, launched Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), militarised the South China Sea, and turned Pakistan into a client state via China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). While GWOT was not the only causal factor that enabled the rise of China, the real post 9/11 winner was Beijing, which received a 20-year free run, while the US and its allies were mired in the Hindu Kush morass.Fast forward to September 2026 and the most incongruous reality is that after all that treasure expended and blood shed, the US withdrew in a shambolic manner from Afghanistan in August 2021 under President Biden. Today, the Taliban is firmly back in the saddle. Ironically, the very entity against whom the global war was launched now rules Afghanistan with a harsh whip.If there is one metric of collective shame, it is the fate of Afghan women and girls. Twenty-five years after the world promised to liberate Afghanistan from medieval barbarism, half its population is banned from education, work, and public life.The second irony is sharper for India. Pakistan, the epicentre of the jihadi terror scourge, has been rehabilitated as a credible regional interlocutor. This rehabilitation has been accelerated under US President Donald Trump. Pakistan's role as mediator in the US-Iran war of 2026, facilitating the Islamabad MoU and now the Mecca Pact, have burnished its profile.As for consequences, the biggest casualty in the aftermath of 9/11 is the loss of US credibility.In 2001, America was a stunned victim with moral authority. In 2003, Washington blundered into Iraq and was deemed guilty of misleading the UNSC. In 2026, it is seen as a petulant, transactional power that has discarded both norm and principle in the use of military force.The same US that launched GWOT against terror has supported what many now call terrorist acts by Israel—the disproportionate destruction rained on Gaza in 2023 and the pre-emptive attack on Iran in June 2026. Iran's abiding support for Hamas and Hezbollah on one hand and the tactical US support to affiliates of the Islamic State have muddied the eco-system nurturing jihadi terrorism. State support to terrorism in different forms is a recurring Faustian bargain.In 2001, UNSC Resolution 1368 gave US action legitimacy. In 2026, the UNSC is paralysed with no resolutions on the Israel-US bombing of Iran, no resolution on Hormuz mining by Tehran, and no resolution on Pahalgam. That is why Pakistan can be a terror sponsor and a peace mediator, for there are no inviolable norms. Clearly, Musharraf's old playbook now has many practitioners.What does this mean for India? First, global sympathy is transient and does not translate into action. Terrorism is fought by national will and proven capability, not coalitions. Second, India must push back against Nuclear Weapon Enabled Terrorism in a resolute manner. The evolution from strategic hesitation in 2001, to restraint in 2008, to surgical strikes in 2016 and 2019, and finally, Operation Sindoor 2025, marks a doctrinal evolution that must be refined.Twenty-five years ago, 9/11 promised a world united against terrorism without distinction. Today, it is more grey and opaque, and pragmatism couched as realpolitik is the preferred option. Delhi has also decided to deal with the Taliban, while holding the line on state sponsored terrorism. But it is a lonely vigil. The US has ostensibly moved on after 9/11, but the scars remain.(C Uday Bhaskar is a leading expert on strategic affairs. He is currently Director, Society for Policy Studies. This is an opinion piece. All views expressed are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for them.)

editorials.title: Postpartum Psychosis Is Real. Why Is Recovery for Indian Mothers Left to Luck?
editorials.passage: (If you know someone or are personally dealing with postpartum mental health issues, know that you are not alone. Reach out to the NIMHANS Perinatal Mental Health Helpline – 8105711277.)A case in the US has the world watching with rapt attention. Lindsay Clancy, a 36-year-old woman from Massachusetts, strangled her three young children in 2023.Her defence said it was postpartum psychosis, while the prosecution argued she knew what she was doing. Twelve jurors sat with the same evidence for days. Unfortunately, unlike the movie 12 Angry Men, there was no Henry Fonda to talk them into agreement. After several days of deadlock, the judge declared a mistrial. Miles away in a drawing room in Mumbai, my friends had already reached a verdict, one which was swift and unanimous. “We can’t take refuge in a condition that isn’t even recognised by the psychiatry bible—the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM).”I let the verdict sit with me for a while, then began my research on the condition, letting the case rest with the jury.'No One Tells You...': New Moms in Kashmir on Battling Postpartum DepressionA woman’s body goes through extreme hormonal and immune shifts after childbirth. Estrogen and progesterone, the hormones that support pregnancy and mood, rise slowly for nine months and then suddenly crash post-childbirth. It’s one of the fastest hormonal falls the human body endures. These changes almost invariably cause "baby blues" characterised by mood swings, tearfulness, and irritability that resolve within days to a couple of weeks.It’s estimated that one in six women go through postpartum depression, a persistent mood disorder marked by sadness, exhaustion, guilt, and loss of interest that doesn’t lift on its own, along with difficulty bonding with the baby. Estimates also point to one in a thousand women going through postpartum psychosis, where they lose touch with reality. This could look like disorganised thinking, seeing or hearing things that aren’t there, false beliefs, or extreme suspicion of people around her.The risk is highest within 12 weeks of childbirth and leaving it untreated carries a rare yet real risk of suicide or infanticide.Both conditions are treatable, yet families often dismiss them as nothing more than "baby blues". An elder woman in the family may brush off the symptoms as normal, something she says she went through herself.The Right to Breastfeed Means Little Without a Place For Mothers to Do ItSo were my friends right? Not quite. Postpartum psychosis is a recognised clinical condition, but it doesn’t appear as a separate diagnosis in the DSM yet. What experts can’t agree on is where it belongs. The DSM sorts mental illnesses into groups, a bit like chapters in a book, and this condition doesn’t neatly fit into any of the existing ones. I spoke to Dr Kersi Chavda, a senior psychiatrist at Hinduja Hospital, on what it means for diagnosing and treating patients while the condition still isn’t in the DSM. “It doesn’t matter if it’s not added to the DSM yet,” Dr Chavda said, adding: “There’s enough research to prove we know this is a condition that needs immediate psychiatric care.”Postpartum psychosis is a recognised condition, but without a clear, distinct place in the diagnostic manual, training and awareness gaps follow. These likely play a part in why many women are still misdiagnosed.Who is more at risk of postpartum psychosis? Those with a family history of mental health disorders, and a personal history of mental illness. Dr Chavda flagged another issue affecting maternal mental health. “Women with pre-existing conditions often pause their psychiatric medication during pregnancy or after childbirth, fearing it will harm the baby. It has been proven that continuing psychiatric medicines under proper guidance is safer for the health of both mother and child than abruptly stopping them,” he said.Dr Sudeshna Ray, associate director of gynaecology at Jaslok Hospital, Mumbai, added, “In some cases, doctors do recommend a brief pause, which is called a ‘drug holiday’ during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, when fetal organ development is most active, but only for women who are doing well and can safely tolerate it. This is always done in consultation with the treating psychiatrist and never decided alone. For everyone else, continuing treatment under medical supervision remains safer than stopping out of fear.”As the gynaecologist is often the first point of contact, her advice to fellow gynaecologists is direct:“Always explicitly ask about mental health history. Look for subtle signs and never miss an opportunity to psychoeducate the family, because it’s a narrow window.”Beyond regular engagement, she also makes it a point to psychoeducate the mother and family on the second day after delivery.‘Breast Not the Best?’: A Mom’s Nursing Journey From Breastfeeding to FormulaResearch shows the ideal treatment setting is a specialised mother-infant unit in a psychiatric facility. When I called over a dozen mental health facilities offering inpatient admission across four major metros in India, most had never heard of the concept. A few offered to informally accommodate mother and baby in a larger room, though I couldn’t establish whether that followed any formal protocol. Most simply treated the mother’s condition as they would any other patient; the infant wasn’t part of the admission at all. After the sixth call, I stopped being surprised. Two facilities in the country came up cleanly in both primary and secondary research as offering these specialised units—NIMHANS, the central government institute based in Bengaluru, and Shadithya Hospital, a private facility in Chennai. Between them, they have a combined capacity of 12 beds. England, with a population roughly one-twentieth of India’s, has around 20 specialised mother-and-baby psychiatric units with over 150 beds. I wonder if, without a formal DSM entry, there’s simply no mandate forcing facilities to plan for optimum care.As I think about the failures stacked at every level, I keep coming back to one question. What are the odds of a woman in this condition actually reaching remission in India? I believe that even for an urban, educated, privileged woman, it takes a near perfect stroke of luck. Lucky that those around her recognise something is wrong and seek help instead of reassurances. Lucky that there’s a psychiatrist close enough to where she lives, one who knows better than to go strictly by the manual and can diagnose it. Lucky, if it comes to that, that a bed is available at all, and lucky that all of this happens fast enough to matter. And if this is what it takes for a woman with every advantage, I don’t know what it takes for a woman with none. What still gives me hope is that NIMHANS’s own published research on its mother-baby unit found that most mothers showed significant improvement by the time of discharge. I wonder who is to blame if a woman doesn’t have that stroke of luck and commits an act in a moment when she is out of touch with reality. I hope that in a Viksit Bharat, it doesn’t have to come to luck at all.(Atika Lamba is an ex-banker, now consults organisations in the mental health space, and is also a practising coach.
